Airline pricing is driven by demand, and demand follows predictable weekly patterns. Business travelers fly Monday mornings and Thursday or Friday afternoons. Leisure travelers fly Friday evenings and return Sunday afternoons. The days with the least demand — and therefore the lowest fares — are Tuesday, Wednesday, and Saturday.

Here is what the aggregate pricing data from Google Flights, Hopper, and airline fare databases consistently shows:

The savings are most pronounced on popular leisure routes (New York to Miami, Chicago to Los Angeles, any route to Las Vegas or Orlando) where weekend demand is highest. On less popular routes or business-heavy corridors, the day-of-week effect is smaller. The practical takeaway: if you have any flexibility, fly out on Tuesday or Wednesday and return on a Tuesday or Wednesday. A couple flying round-trip can save $100 to $400 simply by shifting their travel days.

One important note: these are averages across thousands of routes. Individual route pricing varies based on competition, seasonal demand, and airline capacity decisions. Always compare specific dates using Google Flights rather than assuming Tuesday is cheapest for your exact itinerary.

The old advice about booking flights on a specific day of the week — typically Tuesday at 1 AM — is a myth that has never been supported by data. Airlines use dynamic pricing algorithms that adjust fares thousands of times per day based on demand, competition, and remaining seat inventory. There is no magical booking day.

What does matter is how far in advance you book. Here are the optimal booking windows based on aggregate data from Hopper, Google Flights, and CheapAir analyses of millions of fares:

The general pattern is that prices start high when flights first open (9-11 months out), drop to their lowest point in the 1-3 month window as airlines compete for bookings, then spike in the final 2-3 weeks as remaining seats become scarce. Holiday travel follows a compressed version of this pattern with higher floor prices throughout.

The most reliable strategy is not to try timing the absolute bottom but to set fare alerts and buy when the price drops to a level you consider a good deal. Waiting for a slightly lower fare risks watching prices climb permanently as departure approaches.

The right tools eliminate the need to manually check prices. Here is what works best and how to use each one:

Fare alerts are the single most effective strategy for the time-constrained FI-minded traveler. Set alerts on Google Flights for every trip you are considering in the next 6 months. You will receive email notifications when prices drop, and you can book immediately without daily searching. This passive approach consistently saves $50 to $300 per ticket.

For those building a travel rewards strategy, credit card travel portals (Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Travel, Capital One Travel) sometimes offer slightly better prices than booking direct. More importantly, points earned through everyday spending can cover flights entirely. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into 50,000 points — enough for 1-2 round-trip domestic flights. The FI approach to travel rewards is not to spend more to earn points, but to redirect spending you would do anyway through a rewards-earning card and let the points accumulate passively.

Curious about your financial independence number?

These tools can help you estimate your FI target and plan your next milestone.

Find out how much you need to reach financial independence.

Understand the principles behind FI and how to get started.

Model different scenarios and see when you can retire.

The single biggest predictor of cheap airfare is not when you book or which tool you use — it is how flexible you are with dates and destinations. Google Flights date grid and Skyscanner everywhere search exist specifically to help flexible travelers find the cheapest options. Being willing to fly on a Tuesday instead of a Friday, or to visit Portugal instead of France, routinely saves 30-50% compared to fixed-date, fixed-destination searches. For FI-minded travelers, flexibility is a skill that pays dividends on every trip.

Tuesday and Wednesday are consistently the cheapest days to fly domestically, with fares typically 15-25% below Friday and Sunday prices. Saturday can also be a good value for departures. The savings are largest on popular leisure routes where weekend demand creates the biggest price swings.

No. The idea that booking on Tuesday at midnight gets you the best price is a myth. Airlines adjust prices thousands of times per day using dynamic pricing algorithms. What matters is booking within the optimal window (1-3 months out for domestic flights) and setting fare alerts to catch price drops.

For domestic flights, 1 to 3 months before departure is the sweet spot. For international flights, 2 to 8 months is optimal. Holiday travel should be booked 2 to 4 months ahead. Booking too early (6+ months for domestic) or too late (under 2 weeks) typically results in higher prices.

Sometimes. Spirit, Frontier, and other ultra-low-cost carriers advertise base fares 40-60% below major airlines but charge separately for carry-on bags ($35-$65), seat selection ($5-$50), and other extras. For a traveler with no checked bag and no seat preference, budget carriers save real money. For families or anyone checking bags, compare total cost including all fees — major airlines are often competitive.

Yes. The cheapest times to fly domestically are January (after the 7th), February (excluding Valentine week), early March, late April, September, October, and early November. The most expensive periods are the weeks around Thanksgiving, Christmas, spring break, and the peak summer window from mid-June through mid-August.

Travel rewards cards earn points on everyday spending that can be redeemed for flights. A card earning 2x points on all purchases turns $25,000 in annual spending into enough points for 1-2 domestic round trips. The FI-aligned approach is to use a rewards card for purchases you would make anyway (groceries, gas, utilities) and let points accumulate passively — never spend more just to earn points.

Finding cheap flights comes down to three principles: be flexible with dates (fly Tuesday or Wednesday for 15-25% savings), book in the right window (1-3 months for domestic, 2-8 for international), and let technology do the searching (Google Flights fare alerts catch drops automatically). Combined with a travel rewards card that earns points on everyday spending, these strategies make air travel significantly more affordable without requiring hours of research. Set your alerts, stay flexible, and book when the price is right.

#9021. Are Tangerines Good for You? 5 Health Benefits You Might Love

Tangerines are not just tasty — they’re a powerhouse of nutrients. Packed with tangy flavor and vibrant orange color, these citrus delights offer a host of health benefits. From boosting your immune system to rejuvenating your skin, tangerines are nutrient-rich allies for your well-being. Let’s delve into their nutritional profile and discover why they’re a smart addition to your diet.

Tangerines are nutritional powerhouses. Here’s what each of these little champs pack under their orange belts:

Tangerines are teeny cousins of the orange but with a thinner, easier-to-peel skin. They boast a sweet and juicy flavor and pack a ton of vitamins, particularly vitamin C, as well as minerals like potassium, antioxidants, and dietary fiber.

These tiny bursts of sunshine have many benefits that can significantly enhance your health. Here’s why you might want to make tangerines a regular part of your diet:

Tangerines are loaded with vitamin C, turning them into tiny, tasty guardians for your health. This crucial vitamin supercharges your immune system by enhancing the function and effectiveness of white blood cells, which are essential for fighting off pathogens and infections. By improving the activity and response of these cells, vitamin C helps your body combat a wide range of infections more effectively.

Therefore, regular consumption of these mini-oranges satisfies your taste buds and boosts your body’s defense mechanisms — a win-win!

Want that glow? Tangerines have got you covered. They’re high in potassium, a real game-changer for regulating hydration and balancing fluid levels in your skin cells. This essential mineral keeps your skin cells plump and hydrated, warding off pesky, dry, dull patches.

Plus, potassium supports the removal of toxins and wastes, which means clearer, more radiant skin.

Tangerines are also a fantastic source of vitamin A, which strengthens the outer layer of your skin, smoothing out wrinkles and reducing fine lines. Along with vitamin C, it’s a potent antioxidant, protecting your skin from the damaging and aging effects of free radicals.

Are you having tummy troubles? Tangerines can help with a fiber boost that keeps things moving smoothly along your digestive tract.

These zesty little superheroes are your gut’s new best friends. They’re loaded with fiber that bulks up and softens things down there, making your bathroom visits smooth and speedy. This fruity fix helps manage everything from irregular pit stops to those bloated bleurgh days.

Fiber also balances your gut flora, promoting a healthy microbial environment in your intestines. This balance is crucial for optimal digestion, nutrient absorption, and immune function.

So, grab a tangerine to remedy your belly blues next time your gut feels out of whack.

Tangerines are a dynamo when it comes to battling serious health baddies like cancer and heart disease. These little orange wonders are loaded with flavonoids, natural compounds that help with heart health and cancer prevention.

Flavonoids help relax the blood vessels, lowering blood pressure levels and reducing the strain on your heart. This helps keep your ticker ticking smoothly and reduces the risk of cardiovascular diseases like heart attacks and strokes.

But wait, there’s more! When it comes to cancer, flavonoids mess with the bad guys — cancer cells — stopping them from multiplying and spreading their nonsense around your body.

Keep your peepers sharp with a dose of vitamin A from tangerines. This essential nutrient and compounds like beta-carotene shield your eyes from age-related issues and support healthy vision. It plays a key role in creating rhodopsin, a protein in your eyes that allows you to see in low-light conditions.

Munching on tangerines helps keep your night vision in superhero shape and supports overall eye function, keeping your peepers sharp and responsive.

Furthermore, tangerines contain other essential eye health nutrients, like lutein and zeaxanthin. These antioxidants are found in high concentrations in the retina, where they help filter blue light and prevent oxidative damage, further protecting the eyes from conditions like cataracts.

Sure, tangerines are delish and make your taste buds do a happy dance, but they’re also packed with nutrients that can seriously amp up your well-being.

From giving your immune system a high-five to keeping your heart beating like a healthy drum, tangerines are basically wellness wrapped in a bright orange peel. So, go grab one and make it your main squeeze!

#9020. Renovation delays pose "Notre Dame-like" fire risk for Houses of Parliament

Image by Pandora Pictures courtesy of Shutterstock

A government report has found that risks of a major fire at the Palace of Westminster are rising as health and safety incidents increase at the UK parliament building in London, amid continuing delays to its renovation.

Released last week by the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), the report said that maintenance costs for the UNESCO-listed structure are expected to rise from £1.5 million to £2 million a week if no action is taken. According to the latest report on the restoration, the overall cost of the renovation will rise by £420 million for each year the project is delayed.

Parliament voted in 2018 to vacate the Palace for restoration, however this has been delayed by ongoing disagreements about how fully the House of Commons and House of Lords should leave during the anticipated decades-long renovation.

“Political allergy” to updating the building

According to Public Accounts Committee chair Geoffrey Clifton-Brown, current fire risks could result in “Notre Dame-like flames” at the parliament building, which in 2023 was reported by the committee to be at “constant risk of fire”.

“There has long been a political allergy to gripping the nettle that is R&R [repair and renovation],” Clifton-Brown said.

“Consider the impact of global rolling news footage of Notre Dame-like flames licking out of the building’s roof, resulting in the destruction of our heritage, or worse, injuries or loss of life,” he continued.

“These are not notional possibilities, but real and rising risks which our committee identified three years ago.”

Renovation strategy to be decided by 2030

The report outlines four strategies for the renovation of the building laid out by the R&R Client Board, with one needing to be selected by parliament by 2030 for the programme to progress.

Two of these strategies have been recommended by the board in a bid to speed up the decision-making process. These are fully leaving the building, which is estimated to cost between £11.1 billion to £15.6 billion and take 19 to 24 years, and the partially vacating the building, which is estimated at £19.5 billion to £39.2 billion and could take up to 61 years.

Approving either of these recommendations would require parliamentary approval.

“All options ahead involve extremely high figures with very big ranges,” Clifton-Brown said.

“At a time of national fiscal constraint, we would expect the parliamentary authorities to examine these figures extremely carefully to see how they can be reduced before the vote.”

The PAC’s report also found that there are areas that still need costing, including aspects like decommissioning, relocation of the building’s services, and the restoration of the medieval cloister court.

The cross-party committee has urged the clerks of both House of Commons and House of Lords to set out remaining cost estimates and provide a detailed schedule for the works.

“It is crucial that we preserve the palace as a symbol of our democracy,” the report said. “A failure to act would have serious consequences for taxpayers and future generations.”

The renovation of the adjacent Elizabeth Tower was recently completed by architecture studio Purcell, and last year was awarded a RIBA London award.

#9019. RooMoo transforms abandoned mountain cabins into hotel in China

Concrete drill cores, discarded bricks and timber salvaged from abandoned mountain cabins have been repurposed for a 24-room retreat by Chinese studio RooMoo on Jinfo Mountain in Chongqing, China.

RooMoo transformed a five-level former sales office into the Cloudhaus Hotel, retaining the building’s original structure while incorporating materials collected from the surrounding landscape and nearby villages.

Located at an altitude of 1,200 metres on the mountain’s northern slope, the building has a white-rendered facade punctuated by eight projecting white frames that extend vertically across its elevations.

Bamboo panels and stone slabs fill sections between the frames, while timber detailing and sloping tiled roofs reference traditional buildings in the region.

Rather than using new materials, RooMoo visited local abandoned wooden cabins and furniture workshops to identify resources that could be reused. The studio ended up using timber from the cabins for the project.

“Instead of relying solely on research, we planned most of our conceptual design time to explore the mountains for locally available materials and resources to respect the local environment,” the studio said.

Among the most unusual interventions are walls made from concrete cores extracted during structural renovations, which have been stacked vertically and separated by dark metal supports.

Demolished red bricks were reused in the restaurant, while discarded bamboo scaffolding treads were cut into strips and transformed into ceiling panels and outdoor paving.

The restaurant occupies an expanded podium at the building’s lower level, with indoor dining areas leading towards outdoor terraces.

Its interiors combine stone walls, timber furniture and woven seating, while reclaimed bricks and bamboo offcuts feature in the finishes.

Visitors enter the hotel via the reception on the building’s uppermost floor, which is accessed from an entrance courtyard and connecting bridge.

A timber reception desk sits in front of a wall covered in bamboo panels, woven surfaces and discarded bamboo-shoot shells, which had been harvested locally in the mountains.

Above the lobby, an exposed pitched roof was lined with bamboo and supported by substantial timber beams.

A large woven bamboo installation hangs over the lounge, where black sofas and tan leather chairs were arranged beside full-height glazing overlooking the forested mountains.

Guestrooms were arranged in a fan-shaped layout facing the mountain landscape.

The hotel offers several room types, including courtyard rooms, suites and standard king rooms, with interiors featuring earthy colours, salvaged timber and locally made furniture.

Founded in Shanghai in 2017 by Tao Zhang, Ray Zhang and Marine Bois, RooMoo works across hospitality, restaurant, commercial, office and residential projects.

Other recent interior projects in China include a Linehouse-designed hotel with an industrial feel and a Shanghai tea shop that draws on Rockbund’s historic buildings.

#9018. What's Love Got to Do With It? The Relationship Cycle Explained

Relationships aren’t just about candlelit dinners and cozy sofa nights — they’re complex AF, filled with ups, downs, twists, and turns. From the first flush of love to the settled comfort of commitment, relationships have stages that evolve with time.

Each relationship phase serves a unique purpose, helping you learn more about each other, yourself, and the kind of relationship you want to build. Understanding the dynamics of these stages is crucial for any couple (or throuple!) aiming to develop a lasting bond.

Whether you’re in the throes of a new romance or navigating the challenges of a long-term commitment, continue reading to learn how to rock each phase like a pro.

From those “can’t eat, can’t sleep” early days to the “let’s build an empire” moments, each relationship stage is like a season of your fave drama binge. But, like any good drama, the plot thickens as time passes and things change. Here’s what to expect, month by month:

Welcome to the love bubble, where everything about your significant other seems nothing short of magical. The positives overshadow any negatives, creating a blissfully skewed balance sheet of love. It lasts from about 6 months to 2 years for most peeps, but many folks say they are still madly in love even after 20 years together!

Research shows that during this stage, the prefrontal cortex, which is crucial for critically judging others, shows decreased activity. In other words, you’re less likely to focus on your partner’s faults and more likely to overlook their flaws.

Lurve also activates specific areas in the brain that are driven by goals and rewards. These areas are rich in dopamine and oxytocin receptors, chemicals that make you feel good and bonded to others. They encourage you to pursue and maintain a relationship because it feels rewarding and fulfilling.

If the euphoric stage is the wild, pulse-racing party of love, the early attachment stage is the cozy after-party where things get real comfortable. In the thrilling initial phase, your brain is doped up on dopamine, but as this initial buzz begins to mellow, a more sophisticated part of the brain starts to step up — the ventral pallidum.

Now, after the first year or so, deeper bonds are formed, helped along by attachment hormones like vasopressin and oxytocin, also fondly known as “the love hormone.” These hormones help transform the electric excitement of new love into a warm, enduring attachment.

Hold tight because the crisis stage hits around 5 to 7 years, and it’s a true test of your relationship’s resilience. This phase often feels like a rollercoaster, where life’s challenges can either pull you apart or push you closer together. Many couples experience a drift during this time, and how you handle it — either by addressing the issues head-on or continuing to drift — can define your future together.

Significant life events, like becoming parents, often occur during this stage and can intensify the pressure. These events can either strengthen your bond through shared responsibilities and mutual love or strain it to the breaking point. Successfully navigating this stage means moving beyond mere survival to fostering a deeper, more meaningful connection.

If you’ve made it this far, congrats, you’re in the deep attachment stage! Post-crisis, you’re looking at 7 years and beyond where you settle into that deep, comfy love. No more daily fireworks — now it’s about a slow-burning ember that warms the house.

You know each other inside and out, warts and all. It’s about unconditional support, knowing looks across crowded rooms, and being each other’s rock. Welcome to the good life!

Every relationship is a blend of sweet and sour and everything in between. Understanding the stages, from the initial euphoria to the deep attachment stage, helps you embrace the journey, keep your bond strong, and prepare your heart for whatever comes next. So buckle up and enjoy the ride — it’ll be worth it!

Last medically reviewed on June 26, 2024

#9017. chiaro audio guide app turns smartphone photos of landmarks into 18-language spoken tours

point your phone at a door at notre-dame de paris and chiaro tells you which one it is, then tells its story out loud, in any of 18 languages.

Muhammad edited by christina vergopoulou November 17, 2026 2 min

Chiaro is a mobile audio guide application that generates location- and object-specific narration from user photographs rather than relying on predetermined museum routes or numbered stops. Designed for real-time architectural and cultural exploration, the interface uses visual recognition to identify landmarks and architectural details directly through a smartphone camera, immediately delivering spoken context in 18 languages.

For example, capturing a photograph of an entrance on the west facade of Notre-Dame de Paris prompts the system to identify the structure as the Portal of the Virgin, detailing its carving between 1210 and 1220 and the stacked sculptural reliefs of the death and coronation of the Virgin above. Following the initial overview, Chiaro’s software sequences secondary historical chapters, such as information on the portal’s patronage, while supporting interactive voice or text queries that dynamically generate subsequent audio segments based on user questions.

#9016. Faulty Wedding Cake pavilion to be dismantled at Waddesdon Manor

Photography by Chris Lacey and Merriman Photography

A 12-metre-high pavilion shaped like a wedding cake is set to be dismantled at Waddesdon Manor in Buckinghamshire, UK, after it was closed over health and safety concerns.

A spokesperson for the Grade I-listed country house told the BBC that the pavilion, which was installed in 2023, was not “open for quite as long as hoped” due to faults in its ceramic tiles.

The sculptural pavilion, simply named Wedding Cake, was designed by Portuguese artist Joana Vasconcelos as a permanent garden pavilion for the grounds of Waddesdon Manor.

Its three tiers are wrapped in glazed, pastel-toned ceramic tiles made by the historic Portuguese tile manufacturer Viúva Lamego and intended to look like cake icing. They are now faulty, forcing the structure to close because of concerns about their safety.

A report including photos of the damaged tiles was shared on Buckinghamshire Council’s online planning portal, but the root cause has not been publicly stated.

According to the BBC, a Buckinghamshire Council officer found that no viable solution to repair the faulty tiles had been identified.

As such, the council has approved a change to the listed building consent, allowing the sculpture to be removed. As the manor and its grounds are protected sites, permission must be obtained to carry out such work.

The structure must now be removed no later than January 2036. However, the Rothschild Foundation, which manages the estate, wants the sculpture removed as soon as possible, according to the BBC.

The revised consent also requires the surrounding landscape to be returned to grass within six months of its removal.

When the pavilion was completed, its designer Vasconcelos told Dezeen it was her “most ambitious project to date”.

Her use of tiles reflected her ambition to use ceramics and textiles to challenge traditional hierarchies of what she called “noble materials”, such as marble, in grand architectural settings.

The manufacturer Viúva Lamego’s standard 14-by-14 centimetre tiles determined the size of the overall structure. It has an 11-metre diameter, which was the smallest that could be achieved using the tiles.

The pavilion is the fourth project by Vasconcelos created for the estate, which was built in the 1870s by Baron Ferdinand de Rothschild to entertain guests and showcase his ceramic collections.

A spokesperson for the manor said it plans to continue to commission artwork for its grounds.

“We are hoping to continue to showcase art in the landscape, including plans for a new contemporary sculpture trail in the grounds of Waddesdon Manor, which will open in July 2027,” they said.

Other projects by Vasconcelos featured on Dezeen include a 24-metre-long textile installation for Dior’s Autumn Winter 2023 catwalk show.

Elsewhere, we recently reported on the dismantling of Rike Concert Hall, designed by Italian practice Studio Fuksas. It is being demolished less than 15 years after it was completed, and before ever opening to the public.

Photography by Chris Lacey and Merriman Photography

#9015. Vibration Plate Benefits, According to a Weightlifting Coach

Vibration plates are like mini surfboards that give you a good shimmy while you’re exercising. Though you won’t find a mountain of extensive research behind them, you may be impressed by their possible benefits.

We asked a weightlifting coach to explain and show us how to add good vibrations to our workout routine.

These machines, which look like platforms or scales, are designed to activate something called whole-body vibration (WBV). WBV makes the body work harder by forcing it to contract muscles automatically.

Fans of WBV like to perform classic exercises on top of these machines, including:

Research points to WBV’s ability to boost blood flow.

Weightlifting coach Jarrod Nobbe explains that vibration plates help move blood by stimulating muscle contractions through rapid vibrations.

“The rhythmic contraction and relaxation of muscles help pump blood more efficiently throughout the body,” he says.

As Nobbe adds, movement generally increases blood flow and core temperature, preparing the body for activity. This means vibration plates may be an excellent warm-up activity.

A 2021 study showed that WBV can be an alternative exercise for older adults, boosting the effects of strengthening exercise.

Nobbe says this is because WBV engages muscles in a way that mimics resistance training.

“The vibrations activate and force muscles to contract and relax multiple times per second, which can lead to gains in muscle strength and endurance over time, especially when combined with specific exercises,” he says.

Nobbe points to some anecdotal evidence suggesting that regular use of vibration plates may help boost energy levels, possibly thanks to increased blood circulation and enhanced muscle activation.

“Ultimately, I stand by the idea that movement is medicine,” Nobbe says. “Tons of research already proves that regular physical activity boosts mood, mental health, and promotes energy levels.”

Nobbe says WBV may reduce muscle soreness, stiffness, and inflammation by encouraging blood flow to the muscles. This, he explains, aids in faster recovery post-exercise or injury.

WBV has been shown to improve bone mineral density, which Nobbe points out may positively affect those at risk of osteoporosis.

“The mechanical vibrations stimulate bone cells, potentially leading to increased bone density and strength, delivering the same positive bone health benefits of resistance training,” he says.

“Unfortunately, vibration plates aren’t a one-stop shop for weight loss,” Nobbe says.

He explains that vibration plates alone are unlikely to significantly reduce belly fat without dietary changes and additional exercise.

“While vibration plates can contribute to overall calorie expenditure and muscle activation, targeted fat loss requires a comprehensive approach including diet, cardio exercise, and resistance training,” he says.

These tips will help you stand on your vibration plate with a slight bend at your knee or perform exercises on top of it.

More research is needed around WBV — AKA what happens when you use a vibration plate — but existing smaller research is promising.

Use your machine carefully, and remember to maintain a healthy lifestyle and workout routine.

#9014. EMBT shelters Naples metro station beneath "natural and welcoming" vaulted timber roof

Spanish architecture studio EMBT has completed the Naples Underground Central Station in Italy, contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof.

The station, which is shortlisted in the Infrastructure and transport category of Dezeen Awards 2026, sits within the Centro Direzionale, a business district in Naples designed in the 1970s by Japanese architect Kenzo Tange.

The 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

As EMBT founder Benedetta Tagliabue previously told Dezeen during the station’s construction, the curvilinear timber canopy was designed in direct response to what she called the “artificial” feel of the modernist Centro Direzionale.

“Kenzo Tange designed Centro Direzionale, and he built a very Kenzo Tange-type of city with reflective skyscrapers and a piazza, very 1970s, very clean,” she told Dezeen in 2021.

“It didn’t work because it’s so different from the rest of Naples,” Tagliabue continued. “So the idea of making a new station there and connecting with the new subway line was also to try to introduce a piece of nature and a piece of the original part of Naples into this artificial piece of the city.”

The roof of the station was constructed from arches and beams of glue-laminated (glulam) timber, which are partially supported by the existing concrete structure and shelter a floor finished in local Etna and Trani limestone.

According to Tagliabue, the branching columns and supports of these arches were designed to evoke the feeling of “walking through a forest”, while referencing the arched roofs of historic railway stations.

“We wanted the everyday experience of catching a train to feel more natural and welcoming, giving people a sense of being at home in the middle of the city,” she told Dezeen.

“We were also interested in what wood could bring to this particular neighbourhood. There is so much glass and concrete here; introducing timber was a way of bringing back a connection with nature, through its warmth and texture,” she added.

“The roof follows the geometry of the tracks, so something that is normally hidden underground becomes visible in the shape of the building.”

The vaulted canopy not only shelters the station’s ticket barriers and access routes, but extends towards the new surrounding paved plaza on either side, which faces a church to the north and incorporates new planting to the south.

Below ground, the station platforms are lined entirely with striped panels in bold shades of red, orange and yellow informed by Pompeian frescoes. This theme is continued above ground in the form of colourful silhouettes.

“Our station is not directly above archaeological remains, so we introduced our own references to that history, with a little humour. The reds and yellows recall Pompeii, and figures appear and disappear across the surfaces,” Tagliabue explained.

“I like the idea that a station can offer these unexpected encounters: along the way, you discover something about the city and feel more connected to it,” she added.

Elsewhere in Naples, sculptor Anish Kapoor and architecture studio AL_A previously designed two sculptural station entrances – one in weathered steel and the other in aluminium – as part of a project to connect the underground to the city’s Traiano district.

Other metro station architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the mirrored Qasr AlHokm Metro Station in Saudi Arabia by Snøhetta and the series of buildings created for Melbourne’s Metro Tunnel by studios RSHP, Hassell and WW+P Architects.

#9013. Crosslam completes Brazil's tallest mass-timber tower

Engineering company Crosslam has designed and built Aurora 275, a hybrid building with mass-timber elements that the company claims is the tallest of its type in Brazil.

Standing 22 metres tall, Aurora 275 is considered a hybrid-timber building, with a structural system consisting of a reinforced concrete core, metal, and mass-timber elements including glued-laminated timber (glulam) beams and columns.

Located in the Suzano area of São Paulo, according to Crosslam, it is the tallest building of its type in Brazil.

Crosslam, which usually acts as an engineer for other firms, designed the building itself to demonstrate the potential of mass timber in Brazil.

“We believed that, to sell the first timber building, we first had to build our own,” said Crosslam founder José Alberto Corrêa. “Otherwise, the Brazilian market wouldn’t trust that it was possible.”

To further demonstrate the method’s viability, the building was constructed in four weeks by a five-person team, according to Crosslam. The timber was produced in the company’s factory using wood sourced from Brazil.

Aurora 275 sits next to smaller residential buildings. It features a metal-clad facade, with yellow detailing running up its face.

It extends in two directions from a concrete core, with balconies for each of the 10 apartments.

On the outside, the timber elements are only visible on the undersides of the balconies.

However, on the inside, the timber elements are more visible, with the cross-laminated timber floorplates and glulam beams exposed, giving the interiors a warm feel.

Crosslam said that the structure shows the potential for timber buildings for industrial-style housing production in the country.

“Using engineered timber offers benefits related to the industrialisation of construction, the efficiency of the assembly process, and building performance,” said the project teaam.

“The main advantages include: faster assembly, dimensional precision, reduced waste on the construction site, a lighter structure, and lower carbon emissions.”

The company claimed that the building is carbon neutral.

Timber construction for tall buildings is gaining popularity across the world, with inroads into construction in North America and Europe. The current tallest timber structure in the world recently topped out in Australia.

#9012. kato taverna and ROOVICE strip 1960s tokyo apartment to concrete shell for 50-sqm renovation

the collaborative team organizes apartment’s living, sleeping, and wet zones with lauan plywood, a salvaged stainless-steel kitchen, and mortex finishes.

giulia taverna edited by christina vergopoulou November 17, 2026 4 min

Located in Tokyo’s Setagaya-ku, Gakudai Apartment is the 50-sqm residential renovation of a 1960s top-floor apartment by Tokyo-based designer couple kato taverna, completed in collaboration with Japanese construction firm Roovice. Stripping away a dated remodel from two decades prior that had sealed off windows and created dead zones around existing plumbing shafts and columns, the design team pares the unit back to its raw concrete shell. Organized on a continuous floor level with minimal partitions, the layout separates day and night zones around a central living-dining-kitchen (LDK) core using a restrained material palette of lauan plywood, stainless steel, and mortar.

By installing an insulated entry door, the design studio eliminates the need for a vestibule partition, allowing the enlarged mortar-finished doma, fitted with a custom bench, coat rack, and elastic-rope shoe storage mounted to an exposed concrete column, to open directly into the LDK. In the kitchen, a salvaged Maruzen stainless-steel commercial unit is adapted with adjustable legs, custom lauan plywood internal storage, and a simplified wall exhaust fan to avoid running long ductwork across the ceiling. To visually level the irregular ceiling heights caused by the roof’s drainage slope, a perimeter stainless-steel bar wraps the living area, serving simultaneously as a curtain track and hanging rail.

On the quieter side of the plan, the bedroom is enclosed like a timber box with ceiling and party-wall insulation, an asymmetrical mirrored door fitted directly against the uneven structural column and beam, and a bed frame with concealed storage and custom stainless-steel reading lights. Behind it, a compact study features a fold-away wall desk for dual use as a guest room. In the tight wet zone, replacing a prefabricated unit bath with a Mortex-finished enclosure and a TOTO poly bathtub freed up space to reopen sealed windows, filtering light through glass blocks in the toilet and a sliding rail mirror in the washroom, while wall-mounting the air conditioning units cleared the narrow veranda to function like an engawa.

#9011. Toot Toot! 6 Tips to Prevent Protein Farts

Protein farts are a common, albeit smelly, side effect of high-protein diets. They happen because of how proteins are digested. But(t) don’t worry! We have some tips to help you say goodbye to those pungent protein toots without giving up your gains.

Protein farts are episodes of flatulence that don’t smell too pleasant! They’re generally due to upping your protein intake from supplements like protein shakes.

And while these butt whistles may be embarrassing, you’ll be glad to know they’re generally harmless.

Farts consist of different gases. The most stinky odors usually come from your gut bacteria, producing sulfur-containing compounds as they break down food. The main culprit is hydrogen sulfide, which gives off a characteristic rotten egg smell, yum!

But why do your protein choices lead to thunder from down under?

Well, there’s not much evidence that a high-protein diet causes protein farts. However, there’s some anecdotal evidence that supplementary protein — like protein bars, protein shakes, and powder powders — increases flatulence, but it’s likely due to non-protein ingredients like lactose.

Supplements containing whey protein or casein are derived from milk and are high in lactose, which can increase flatulence. If your body can’t properly digest lactose, it ends up in your colon, where bacteria feast on it, producing — you guessed it — more gas and cheek flapping.

So, whey protein can throw a curveball for those who are lactose intolerant or sensitive. Surprisingly, it might also stir up digestive drama even for folks who typically handle dairy like champs, potentially due to additives like fart-inducing sweeteners or thickeners.

Some people may also have more significant issues digesting protein. Proteins are big, complex molecules — breaking them down is no small task for your gut. Plant-based protein supplements, like those based on soya beans, may also worsen flatulence.

FYI: Another reason why flatulence is common with protein powders and supplements is due to the addition of artificial sweeteners in the powders and bars, like sugar alcohols, sucralose, sorbitol, xylitol, and stevia.

If you’re looking to continue your protein regimen without becoming a walking, talking whoopee cushion, here are some strategic adjustments you can make:

Don’t just dive into the deep end with your protein intake — wade in slowly. Gradually increasing the amount of protein you consume allows your digestive system to adjust without getting overwhelmed. This step-by-step approach can help minimize the likelihood of excessive gas.

Keep the water flowing. Drinking plenty of water is crucial as it helps your digestive system handle higher protein levels more efficiently. Proper hydration aids in the breakdown and absorption of nutrients, which can help prevent gas buildup.

Sometimes, your body needs a little extra help. Enzyme supplements like Beano or Lactaid can be game-changers, especially if you consume proteins that your body struggles with. These supplements help break down proteins and lactose, making digestion smoother and less gassy.

Variety isn’t just the spice of life — it can also be the solution to your protein fart problems. If whey protein tends to upset your stomach, explore other options like plant-based or animal-based proteins that might be easier to digest. Diversifying your protein sources can also ensure you get a broad range of nutrients.

What you blend your protein powder with can make a big difference. If you’re whipping up a protein shake, be mindful of adding high-fiber fruits and vegetables, as these can also increase gas production. Try to find a balance that allows you to enjoy the benefits of protein and fiber without the extra flatulence.

Introducing probiotics into your diet can improve your gut health, which can help manage and reduce gas production. Whether through supplements or probiotic-rich foods like yogurt, kefir, or sauerkraut, boosting your gut flora can aid in better overall digestion and less discomfort from gas.

Protein farts are a rather windy side effect of a high-protein diet, but they don’t have to knock you off course. Try easing into your protein consumption, staying hydrated, diversifying your protein sources, and integrating enzyme supplements or probiotics to max those gains, minus the stink bombs!

#9010. Finnegan Shannon installs conveyor belt for displaying art accessibly in Brooklyn

New York City-based artist Finnegan Shannon has installed a conveyor belt to display art at cultural centre Pioneer Works in Brooklyn, USA, as a commentary on accessibility in art.

According to Pioneer Works, the There’s No Me Without You installation fulfils Shannon’s “longtime fantasy of an exhibition space that would meet their access needs”.

Chairs were placed around the closed-loop 12-foot-long mechanism, letting visitors sit when viewing and engaging with exhibited objects, archival materials and portable DVD players placed on a series of moving trays.

It was created from a restaurant-style system similar to those used in sushi restaurants where the food is delivered via a conveyor belt. The rest of the room on the upper floor of the arts centre was covered in rich fabrics and built-in benches along the perimeter.

“My conveyor belt, technically a retail and restaurant-style display system, is a tool for me to be in less pain when I’m experiencing art,” said Shannon, who is disabled. “I notice I am a much more patient and curious visitor when I’m sitting down.”

The title of the installation reflects the artist’s relationship to the concept of interdependence.

“If disabled people were in charge, we would have a bunch of varied and deluxe options for sitting and lying down in exhibition spaces,” they said.

“Instead we live in a world where this type of infrastructure is quite basic and sparse.”

The installation is being used to present new commissions by artists with disabilities Joselia Rebekah Hughes, Ariana Martinez and Alex Dolores Salerno. For the three consecutive exhibitions, visitors are invited to interact with the work through touch, sight, and sound.

Air filters with bright colours were included in the middle of the conveyor belt to assist with air quality and masks were encouraged for visitors.

Shannon emphasised the collaborative nature of artistic endeavour through the exhibition.

“We know that on some fundamental level, no solo exhibition is truly a solo endeavor,” Shannon said.

“Putting together an exhibition takes immense collaboration and support – art handlers, facilities staff, curators, registrars, accountants, assistants – and that is all within the institution.”

“You can trace that entanglement further: I’m dependent on workers, paid and unpaid care labor, and friendships, family, and more, both locally and across the globe.”

“I never want someone to come away from an exhibition with my work feeling like they’ve experienced something that is mine,” they said. “Instead I hope they have threads to follow to learn more about the vast world of knowledge that is disability culture.”

Shannon’s other projects have focused on access. Alt Text as Poetry, a collaboration with Bojana Coklyat exploring image description and Do You Want Us Here or Not is a series of museum benches and cushions designed to encourage rest.

Other designs that prioritise accessibility were showcased at The Fashion Institute of Technology’s Adapt/Evolve exhibition in New York last year.

There’s No Me Without You is on show at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn from 12 September to 20 December. For more exhibitions, installations and talks worldwide, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

#9009. Undercuts for Women: Benefits, Styles, and Types

Is it time to give your hairstyle and scalp a breath of fresh air? Say hello to the undercut hairstyle, a fashion-forward solution that can elevate your look and promote skin health.

By significantly reducing hair volume, undercuts allow for improved air circulation around the scalp. The result? Less trapped heat and moisture — factors that can contribute to fungal infections, scalp acne, dandruff, and dermatitis.

Whether you’re battling irritation or want to give your “do” a new lease on life, continue reading to learn how undercut hairstyles can be your ally in style and scalp health.

An undercut involves shaving or cutting hair very short on the sides or back of the head while leaving the hair on top longer.

Originally popular in men’s hairstyling, the undercut has crossed gender boundaries and gained popularity among peeps seeking a hairstyle that stands out.

It’s a style that offers a stark contrast and is often used to add an edge to an otherwise conventional look. So whether it’s a side undercut, undercut pixie, mullet undercut, or nape undercut, these hairstyles for women, men, and folks of all genders enhance individuality while offering practical benefits like reduced drying time and less hair maintenance.

Choosing an undercut means embracing a hairstyle with a “heady” mix of aesthetic and practical benefits. Here’s why an undercut might be the refreshing change you need.

Ready to turn heads? The standout feature of an undercut is undoubtedly its unique appearance. Hidden under the longer layers, it packs a punch of boldness you can flaunt or conceal — whatever fits your vibe. You can control the reveal, whether you’re showcasing that edgy undercut for a night out or keeping it classy for the office.

Got a mane that’s more lioness than laid-back? An undercut might be your new BFF. Strategically shaving or trimming the hair short on the sides or back dramatically dials down the volume. This means your thick, voluminous hair becomes way easier to manage and style, turning a heavy head of hair into something light and breezy.

And the best part? You get to keep all the styling potential without any of the hassle. It’s a practical solution that doesn’t sacrifice style for comfort.

Are you chasing the clock every morning? An undercut could slash your prep time. With less hair to fuss over, you can breeze through your washing, drying, and styling routine faster than you can say “snooze button.”

This trimmed-down approach is a time-saver and reduces the daily wear and tear from blow dryers and straighteners, keeping hair healthier in the long run.

Undercuts reduce your scalp’s weight and improve hair follicle airflow. This keeps the scalp cooler and reduces the buildup of sweat and oil that can lead to scalp irritation, dermatitis, and dandruff. As a result, undercuts could lead to more robust, healthier hair growth.

Ready to shake up your style with a cool undercut? Here’s a rundown of some options to add a dash of daring to your daily look:

Are you looking for a dramatic change without total commitment? Try the side-swept undercut.

This style features a sleek shave on one side of the head, just above the ear, while keeping the hair on top and the other side longer.

It’s perfect for folks who love to play with contrast — sweep the top hair over to the shaved side for an instant bold statement.

If subtlety is more your speed, this undercut is a wicked choice. It’s a shaved area tucked away at the back of the head or underneath the top layer of hair so that it can play a fantastic game of hide-and-seek.

Wear your hair down for a business-as-usual look, or tie it up to reveal a sneaky, stylish surprise. It’s an excellent choice for peeps wanting a touch of edge.

Are you feeling bold and artistic? Design Undercuts take personal expression to the next level. These chic undercuts are masterpieces, boasting intricate geometric patterns, sweet floral motifs, or any design that speaks to you.

Do you prefer a more understated yet stylish look? The tapered undercut starts very short near the ear and gracefully lengthens as it ascends the head, blending with your other locks.

It’s a softer version of the undercut that pairs beautifully with bob or lob cuts and offers a gentle nod to the undercut trend without going full-throttle.

The undercut hair offers both style and substance. It reduces styling time and promotes scalp health. By alleviating the weight and allowing the scalp to breathe, undercuts can help minimize issues like overheating and irritation, especially during warmer months.

Whether you’re drawn to the edgy designs or the subtle tapered style, an undercut could be a clever hack to simplify your morning routine. More time for coffee, less time with the comb!

#9008. Pablo Castillo partners with Decibel on 3D-printed chair with under-seat storage

A bookshelf slots in below the cantilevered seat of Kino, a 3D-printed chair developed by Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo.

Castillo designed Kino for Decibel, an American company that specialises in 3D-printed furniture and installations. It is shortlisted for seating design of the year in the upcoming Dezeen Awards.

The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.

The chair is essentially a monobloc, with a single component forming the T-shaped seat, two legs, the shelf and a curved backrest.

Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.

Decibal also offers an outdoor version printed from recycled PETG, a thermoplastic polyester.

“I wanted the substantial thickness of the plastic and the way it builds a product layer by layer to translate into features that give the chair its character,” Castillo told Dezeen.

“Following this line of thought allowed me to move beyond mere dimensions and general ergonomic considerations,” the designer said.

“The cantilevered seat, the under-seat storage, and specific details such as the T-junctions naturally emerged.”

The seat’s T-shape was created by cantilevers both forwards and backwards. This makes the chair less rigid than a typical 3D-printed chair, improving comfort.

“By reinforcing the lower part of the seat with a corrugated structure integrated directly into the 3D print, we achieved a chair that offers a slightly broader range of motion than a traditional design,” Castillo said.

“It seamlessly accommodates highly reclined, relaxed postures, as well as more active positions when the user leans forward.”

Kino joins Decibel’s Editions collection, which also includes chairs by designers including Charles Birshaw, Karim Rashid and Deniz Aktay.

The New Jersey-based brand launched this collection with an exhibition at the Alcova show in Milan in 2025, when it was live-printing chairs in the former SNIA factory in Varedo.

The chairs are produced using a Caracol robotic 3D printer, which allows geometries that wouldn’t be possible with injection moulding.

#9007. james bridle and the power of solar, zooplankton, and non-human entities

ancient symbols and microscopic organisms meet contemporary solar technology in an artistic reflection on energy, ecology, and coexistence.

annalise kamegawa November 17, 2026 7 min

Back in 2022, James Bridle—artist, technologist, and author of the book New Dark Age (2018)—created a work called Solar Panels (Radiolaria Series). It was a series of five functional 100W photovoltaic generators, the faces of which were etched with tiny, microscopic zooplankton called Radiolaria. Looking at images of their silica skeletons, enlarged hundreds of times so they are visible to the human eye, reveals a universe of spiky arms, swirling bodies, intricate lattices, and geometric patterns. Juxtaposed with each other, and containing their own advanced modes of capturing energy, Bridle creates a compelling parallel between non-human and human intelligence, and what that could mean for the future of the earth.

Across their writing, installations, and lectures, James Bridle has become known for thinking about the ways that technology, the natural world, and humanity influence each other, with a strong emphasis on understanding ‘intelligence’. They look beyond the popular, mainstream ideas associated with the word, often linked to IQ, large language models, and other forms of reconstructing human thought patterns. In their piece, AI was built on human intelligence. Nature has more to teach, they express the urgency of going beyond this definition, and to learn from the other creatures we share the Earth with.

It is this line of thinking that has underwritten their works with solar panels, water collection systems, and vernacular architecture. Looking back to their 2019 exhibition, Through Other Eyes, which they curated with NeMe Art Centre in Cyprus, an emphasis on more-than-human forms of thinking and creating is evident. Here, they invoked the 1922 writing of Dziga Vertov, in which he describes his fascination with documentation through the lens of a camera. Bridle parallels this with the technologies of the twenty-first century – all the mania, fascination, and consequences – saying that, if we apply these new or different ‘eyes’, those of machines and animals, ‘They might also, if we are open to them, offer us visions of unexpected insight, and startling beauty.’ It is within this vision – trans-species and trans-machine – that Bridle’s work takes form.

Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell AnyoneThings Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone

Putting an image of radiolaria on a solar panel conjures ideas about the ability to sustain life and other modalities of using energy generated by natural processes. It calls into question the human need to consume power. Radiolaria, microscopic yet possessing highly advanced skeletal structures, can exist symbiotically with algae that provide them with energy. There is an ancient logic to their existence that can be traced back to the Cambrian. Bridle, in their description of the project, highlights how they were ‘famously illustrated, by the German naturalist Ernst Haeckel, who coined the term “ecology” in 1866.’ The complex structures of these organisms continue to inspire wonder, demonstrating how something so small can be so powerful and complex.

Expanding this logic to the scale of solar panels, a technologically intensive mode of capturing and converting energy from the sun in a way that can power human inventions calls into question the effectiveness of human ‘technology’ when compared to that of the non-human. Here is an incredible invention that can create sustainable energy, a promising alternative to fossil fuels, yet it takes advanced electronics and logistics to achieve what a single-celled organism has been doing for thousands of years. Here, Bridle once again asks us to consider what innovation means, not when we compare it to the span of human history.

In 2023, Bridle expanded on the concept in Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, an installation on the archaeological site of Elefsina in Greece, Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone, just north of Athens. Instead of radiolaria, the images engraved on three 100W solar photovoltaic panels are ‘the wheatsheaf, the poppy, and the calathus,’ which ‘honor the ancient cult of Demeter, and the veneration of the living Earth which she represents.’ Here, the comparison of contemporary power generation with beliefs in ancient deities asks us to question the ways in which energy is created, used, and distributed. Bridle used solar panels to power other works in the installation and the site itself, going on to remark that ‘The technology to do these things, is available to us, and the knowledge of how to do them is not a mystery, nor a secret, but it might require new rituals, and new initiations, to distribute it more widely. This is one of those rituals.’

the poppy that would be inscribed on Bridle’s solar panelssketch of Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, an installation on the archaeological site of Elefsina in Greece, Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone by James Bridle

Ultimately, James Bridle’s solar panel creations reflect a broader vision of posthuman utopias that runs throughout their artistic practice: one in which technology, humanity, and the natural world exist in a more reciprocal relationship. By bringing together ancient natural intelligence and contemporary technologies, Bridle challenges human exceptionalism and conventional ideas of progress. Their work encourages us to look beyond ourselves for models of innovation, recognizing that the natural world already holds sophisticated forms of knowledge. In doing so, they invite us to imagine futures founded on ecological interdependence, collaboration, and coexistence.

Things Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell AnyoneThings Said, Things Seen, and Things Done, by James Bridle at Mystery 19 Visual Arts Initiator III – But Don’t Tell Anyone | image by Vangelis Gkinis

#9006. Texas antique and design show unveils new exhibition building made from salvaged materials

Photography by Marburger Farm and Ethan Good Photography

Texas-based antique and design show Marburger Farm has unveiled an exhibition building made partly from salvaged materials sourced directly from across the 43-acre property, as shown in this video produced by Dezeen.

Called Gage Hall, the building’s facade is made from reclaimed timber sourced from around the farm and is topped with a traditional Texas metal roof and contemporary skylight elements that bring natural light into the hall.

The hall brings an additional 7,500 square feet of shopping space to Marburger Farm, bringing the fair’s total space to 100,000 square feet. Designed to honour the site’s dairy farm heritage, the hall also showcases its vision for the future.

The antique and design show has become a destination for international designers looking to source unique interior objects including furniture, lighting and vintage textiles.

The 43-acre show is located in Round Top, Texas, and has attracted designers such as Kelly Wearstler and Leanne Ford.

The fair offers visitors access to objects from over 200 independent dealers and has become one of the largest antique shows in the United States.

The site also includes a Texas-style town square, 10 restored historic buildings, four tents and a 150-year-old saloon, which has been restored to its original use as a social space and bar.

Founded in 1997, the show has grown to attract over 30,000 people annually.

The antique show takes place in January, March and October each year.

Marburger Farm is owned by Brook Partners, a Dallas-based investment company focusing on culture and commerce.

The company also runs the upcoming Dallas Art Fair, which is held from 15 to 18 April 2027 in Dallas, Texas. To learn more, visit the Marburger Farm website.

Marburger Farm Antique Show took place from 27 to 31 October in Round Top, Texas. The winter show will take place 21-24 January and the spring show will take place 23-27 March 2027. See Dezeen Events Guide for an up-to-date list of architecture and design events taking place around the world.

#9005. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

Most estate planning advice assumes you will work until 60-65, accumulate wealth gradually, and have employer-provided benefits until Medicare kicks in. The FIRE path breaks every one of those assumptions. You may stop working at 35, 40, or 50 — meaning your estate plan must cover a potentially 40 to 50-year retirement, not the 20 to 25-year retirement conventional planning addresses.

This extended timeline creates unique vulnerabilities:

The SECURE Act fundamentally changed how inherited retirement accounts work, and this change matters enormously for FIRE households that have built large tax-advantaged portfolios.

Before the SECURE Act, non-spouse beneficiaries could "stretch" inherited IRA distributions over their own lifetime, allowing decades of tax-deferred growth. Now, most non-spouse beneficiaries must withdraw the entire inherited IRA balance within 10 years of the original owner's death. For a beneficiary in their peak earning years, this compressed timeline can push them into the 32% or 37% tax bracket on every distribution.

The FIRE advantage: Early retirees have years — sometimes decades — of lower taxable income between leaving work and taking Social Security or required minimum distributions. This creates a golden window for Roth conversions that no conventional retiree has.

A married couple who retires at 40 with $1.5 million in a traditional 401(k) and a $500,000 Roth IRA could systematically convert $80,000 to $100,000 per year from the traditional to the Roth, staying within the 22% bracket. Over 15 years, they convert $1.2 million to $1.5 million at a known, relatively low tax rate. Their heirs then inherit a Roth IRA that is completely tax-free — even under the SECURE Act's 10-year distribution rule.

Without conversions, those heirs would owe ordinary income tax on every dollar withdrawn from the inherited traditional IRA, potentially at 32% or higher if they are working professionals during their peak earning years. The tax savings for heirs can easily exceed $200,000 to $400,000 on a $1.5 million inherited traditional IRA.

Key Roth inheritance rule: Inherited Roth IRAs are still subject to the 10-year distribution rule, but the distributions are tax-free. The 10-year clock starts the year after the original owner's death.

A revocable living trust is the foundational estate planning tool for FIRE households. It provides three critical benefits that matter more for early retirees than conventional retirees:

Every early retiree needs three healthcare documents executed before leaving their employer:

Once you cross the $1 million net worth threshold — common in the FIRE community — asset protection becomes essential. You have decades of retirement ahead during which a lawsuit, car accident judgment, or liability claim could threaten the wealth you worked so hard to build.

For FIRE households pursuing charitable giving, a donor-advised fund (DAF) allows you to front-load charitable deductions in high-income years (or Roth conversion years), reduce your taxable estate, and distribute grants to charities over time. A DAF contribution is irrevocable and immediately reduces your estate while giving you advisory control over future grants.

Do not wait until traditional retirement age to complete your estate plan. The moment you leave employer benefits, you need a fully executed will or trust, healthcare directives, powers of attorney, updated beneficiary designations, and umbrella insurance. Many FIRE retirees leave their jobs with $1 million or more in assets and no estate plan in place. Every day without these documents is a day your family is exposed to probate, court-appointed guardianship, and preventable tax consequences.

Absolutely. If you have any assets, dependents, or strong preferences about medical care, you need at least a will, healthcare directive, and power of attorney. If you have reached FI with $500,000 or more in assets, a revocable living trust adds significant value through probate avoidance and incapacity protection.

Most non-spouse beneficiaries must now withdraw the entire inherited IRA or 401(k) within 10 years of the original owner's death. This compressed timeline can push heirs into high tax brackets. Roth conversions during your lifetime eliminate this tax burden because inherited Roth IRA distributions are tax-free.

For most early retirees, transferring your primary residence to a revocable living trust makes sense. It avoids probate on the home, enables seamless management if you become incapacitated, and does not affect your mortgage, property tax, or homestead exemption in most states. Consult your estate attorney about your state's specific rules.

Umbrella insurance provides liability coverage above the limits of your auto and homeowners policies. A $1 million umbrella policy typically costs $200 to $300 per year and protects against lawsuits, car accident judgments, and liability claims that exceed your underlying policy limits. For FIRE households with significant assets, it is one of the most cost-effective forms of protection available.

Yes, and early retirement is often the best time to do them. With no employment income, your taxable income is low, allowing you to convert traditional IRA or 401(k) balances to Roth at the 10%, 12%, or 22% bracket. This is significantly cheaper than the 32% or 37% rate your heirs might pay on inherited traditional IRA distributions.

Review your estate plan every three years at minimum and immediately after any major life event: marriage, divorce, birth of a child, death of a beneficiary, significant change in net worth, or a move to a new state. Early retirees have a longer planning horizon, making regular updates even more important than for conventional retirees.

Estate planning for early retirees is not a modified version of conventional retirement planning — it is a fundamentally different discipline. You face a longer incapacity window, a bigger healthcare gap, more exposure to tax law changes, and decades of asset protection needs. The FIRE community excels at building wealth through savings rate optimization and investment discipline. Apply that same rigor to your estate plan: execute foundational documents before leaving your job, optimize beneficiary designations for the SECURE Act, pursue Roth conversions during low-income years, and protect your assets with umbrella insurance and trust structures. The wealth you built deserves a plan that survives as long as your retirement.

#9003. designboom listens: the sounds behind alastair philip wiper’s industrial visions

moving between personal memories, unexpected visual references, and the energy of disco, wiper reveals how music accompanies his work and everyday life.

An album cover encountered in childhood can stay with you for decades. In the case of photographer and creative director Alastair Philip Wiper, the mirrored industrial landscape on The Alan Parsons Project’s Ammonia Avenue became a lasting reference and, eventually, an inspiration for his work. Based in Copenhagen, Wiper turns his camera toward factories, laboratories, scientific equipment, and industrial infrastructures, finding unexpected beauty in the systems people build and the often-absurd ways they operate. His photographs reveal the unexpected visual qualities of places built for function, drawing attention to their symmetry, patterns, and overlooked details.

This week on designboom listens, Wiper shares the music that accompanies his creative moments, moving between disco, jazz, electronic music, and 1980s pop. Some tracks are tied to personal memories, like Cannonball Adderley’s Autumn Leaves, which he played while trying to get his first son to sleep, while others help him find energy or shift his mood. ‘I need something to get me excited and get some energy going. Disco usually does that for me,’ he says of Sister Sledge’s Lost in Music. Kraftwerk’s Radioactivity connects with a book he is currently working on about nuclear technology and culture, while Billy Idol’s Eyes Without a Face echoes some of the more uncanny subjects he has photographed, from robotics to medical and scientific research. Read on for Wiper’s answers and discover the sounds, memories, and visual references behind his practice, then listen to the full playlist below.

What song best captures your creative practice?

Alastair Philip Wiper (APW): Wonderful Life – Black. There are a lot of times when I think I have a wonderful life when working. Not all the time. But then I can just put this song on and I would be back to my wonderful life.

What is the very first track you play to clear the air and get inspired when starting a new project?

APW: Lost in Music – Sister Sledge. I need something to get me excited and get some energy going. Disco usually does that for me.

Is there a song that instantly takes you back to a specific memory or place from your past?

APW: Autumn Leaves – Cannonball Adderly. I played this all the time when I was trying to get my first son off to sleep as a baby, 15 years ago. I would rock him in my arms and bop slowly around the room. Sometimes it worked, a lot of the time it didn’t but I still love it.

What song is stuck in your head right now?

APW: The Captain of Her Heart – Double. Can’t get enough of this 80s beauty.

What is your ultimate 2 AM studio track — the one you secretly know every word to?

APW: Runaround Sue – Dion & The Belmonts. If you want to see me karaoke like an idiot this is probably it.

What song do you put on when you’re stuck and need a breakthrough?

APW:  If You Really Love Me – Stevie Wonder. I’m a massive Stevie Wonder fan and I could have chosen many of his tunes to lift me up, but settled on this. Always puts me in a good mood.

What track is dominating your speakers this week, and is it influencing what you’re making right now? APW: You Always Start it – XXXY. I tend to listen to this tune on repeat for a while, then have a break, then come back to it after a year or so. It’s back this week.

What song helps you slow down and focus on the tiny, quiet details? APW: Within – Daft Punk. I listen to a lot of modern classical like Michael Nyman or Philip Glass when I am trying to focus but want something in the background, but today I decided on this slow one by Daft Punk.

If people were wearing headphones while experiencing your latest work, what one song should be playing? APW:  Radioactivity – Kraftwerk. I’m working on a book about nuclear technology and culture and I love Kraftwerk so it has to be this one.

What is your favorite album cover art? APW:  Island Life – Grace Jones. Jean-Paul Goude is one of my all-time favorite photographers. He was the boyfriend of Grace Jones and was responsible for her whole image around the time she was about the coolest person in the world. All the cool images you have seen of her, looking super sharp, androgynous, robot-like – are down to him. He used to cut up negatives and stitch them together to exaggerate her features – for this image he extended her legs and arms so she seems like a sculpture. Also, The Alan Parsons Project – Ammonia Avenue. I saw this when I was a kid – a photo of some industrial facility which has been mirrored. It stuck with me forever and has been an inspiration for the kind of work I do today.

What track best describes your favorite project you’ve worked on so far? APW: Eyes Without A Face – Billy Idol.  I’ve done a lot of work with sex dolls and robots and cryonics and surgery.
