#9002. Gen Z apps inform approachable wayfinding for V&A East Storehouse

On a mission to draw in museum sceptics, Hackney design studio Fieldwork Facility looked to an unexpected source of inspiration when creating the Dezeen Award-shortlisted wayfinding for London’s V&A East Storehouse.

The landmark museum, completed by Diller Scofidio + Renfro last May, has been lauded for opening up the V&A‘s storage vault, including 250,000 historic art, craft and design objects, to the public for the first time.

The challenge for Fieldwork Facility was to help visitors navigate and interpret this trove of artefacts – especially a younger, more diverse crowd who might normally feel excluded from museums.

To speak to this demographic, studio founder Robin Howie decided to borrow a visual language they’re already intimately familiar with.

“We studied popular Gen-Z apps and services to understand how to make Storehouse feel intuitive as soon as you walk through the door,” Howie told Dezeen.

“Cultural institutions can all too often feel like exclusive environments with many barriers to entry. It’s unfortunately far too easy for so many people to walk into a museum, gallery or national organisation and feel a queasy sense of ‘this isn’t really for me’.”

As an antidote, Howie and his team decided to treat the wayfinding design like an operating system in itself, looking to the UX of much-used apps like TikTok to inform signage and interaction points across the museum.

From the get-go, visitors are welcomed with an “onboarding text” that introduces them to the Storehouse and how to navigate it.

“It’s a moment that purposefully feels like opening an app for the first time where you are given a quick orientation of the experience held inside,” said Howie.

The text combines a range of different media, including printed typography, ticker tape screens and recycled paper tiles.

Topped with recycled plastic letterforms, these tiles provide a first introduction to three key colours used to mark different areas across the building.

Yellow points out viewing galleries, green is for the museum’s viewable restoration labs and pink for the Study Centre, which gives the public unprecedented access to the collection through the V&A’s Order an Object programme – a service traditionally reserved for researchers and academics.

Set into aluminium cases, these recycled paper tiles were used to form adaptable, modular signage across the building. Much like a Scrabble tile, each is emblazoned with a single letter, allowing museum staff to adapt the wayfinding based on what objects are currently on view.

“Storehouse’s signage system looks and feels programmable in an analogue way,” said Howie.

To suit the use across separate tiles, Fieldwork Facility commissioned a bespoke version of the V&A’s brand typeface Spiller that is monospaced.

This technique, normally used for typesetting computer code, involves shaping each letter so it occupies the same amount of horizontal space.

“The resulting Spiller Mono helps give V&A East its own unique language that is atypical for a museum,” Howie said.

“We also love that monospace typefaces were widely used in early computers and are still standard for writing and editing code – great nod to the ‘building as software’ concept.”

On some signs, a colourful, enamelled lava-stone disc provides colour coding, echoing the yellow, green and pink first introduced in the onboarding text.

Several other interventions were also designed to encourage interaction, either from visitors or from staff, who engage with the building both as a museum and an active storehouse.

To provide museumgoers with context and explanation about the pieces on show, Fieldwork Facility created interpretation labels that exist as a modular kit of components, allowing them to be fixed to Storehouse’s standardised crates, palettes and forklift-accessible shelving. Digital templates allow staff to amend these labels without relying on the designers.

The design studio even introduced dedicated “expression points” where visitors can share their opinion with the V&A staff or take part in public polls using a voting coin system.

“The operating system approach welcomes everyone to explore, define their own experience, make connections and have agency within a national institution,” Howie said.

All of the museum’s signage was designed to be adapted and reused to cut out waste, with icons for permanent fixtures – such as toilets, elevators and floor numbers – screen printed or painted directly onto the walls instead of relying on disposable vinyl decals.

Fieldwork Facility’s graphics for V&A Storehouse East have been shortlisted for graphic design of the year at the 2026 Dezeen Awards. It is up against seven other projects, including the visual identity for Dorte Mandrup’s Arctic whale watching facility and ink-free tea packaging for a Song Dynasty-themed restaurant in Guangzhou.

#9001. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

#9000. Studio Octopi revives art deco pavilion and lido on Scottish coast

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson

The restoration of an art deco pavilion and lido near MacDuff, Aberdeenshire, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film is the latest in a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are shown the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion, revived by London-based Studio Octopi to bring its tea pavilion and pools fully back into use.

The studio aimed to retain the historic character of the 1930s art deco building, while introducing considered upgrades, including a marble-clad exterior.

“We wanted to pay homage to the art deco period, which the building was originally conceived in,” said Studio Octopi director James Lowe.

“The green came about really in connection with the paint samples that we took off the railings, and it was decided to go with marble that would give resilience to the environment.”

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Edinburgh Futures Institute by Bennetts Associates.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

#8999. L-Tyrosine Supplements: Benefits for Your Brain and Body

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#8997. DFA awards 2026 turn regional heritage into global design

grounded in cultural lineage yet operating globally, this year's laureates at the DFA awards 2026 span architecture, material innovation, spatial hospitality, and electric mobility.

mariana rodrigues November 17, 2026 6 min

From sculptural jewelry and spatial architecture to material science and electric mobility, the DFA Awards 2026 place Asian design perspectives at the center of the global conversation. Looking outward while remaining anchored in local sensibilities, this year’s honorees prove that cross-disciplinary craftsmanship and territorial memory are quietly reshaping how the world creates.

Spanning diverse creative practices, the recognized designers merge rigorous technical research with deep cultural intuition, offering tangible solutions and distinct visual languages for an interconnected creative landscape.

Founded in 2003 by the Hong Kong Design Centre, the DFA Awards take root in a city shaped by cross-cultural exchange. Supported by the Cultural and Creative Industries Development Agency, the platform connects regional craft with global markets. From the international stage of Business of Design Week to the DX design hub in Sham Shui Po, Hong Kong operates as an active testbed amplifying Asian perspectives across the wider creative landscape.

The program divides its focus across key pillars of contemporary practice, tracing both lifetime legacies and emerging directions. Sustained contributions to spatial discourse, society, and education in Asia receive the DFA Lifetime Achievement Award (LAA), while the DFA Design Leadership Award (DLA) spotlights leaders who deploy design as a catalyst for viable enterprise. International influence rooted in heritage takes center stage with the DFA World’s Outstanding Chinese Designer (WOCD), honoring creators of Chinese lineage commanding global attention.

Regional collaboration and community stewardship define the DFA Designer of the Year (DOY), complemented by the DFA Asian Design Vanguard (ADV), which champions forward-looking practitioners shaping modern industry. Anchoring the framework, the DFA Design for Asia Awards (DFAA) survey built projects, objects, and visual communication that draw directly from regional cultures to elevate daily life and inform future creative output. Looking toward the next generation, the DFA Hong Kong Young Design Talent Award (YDTA) recognizes emerging practitioners in 2026 focused on environmental sustainability and social responsibility, supporting 18 of them to pursue work or study opportunities abroad and bring global insights back to the local creative scene.

The DFA Lifetime Achievement Award (LAA) honors Yung Ho Chang, founding partner of Atelier Feichang Jianzhu and Dean and Chair Professor of Architecture at the University of Hong Kong. Returning to China after graduating from UC Berkeley, Chang cofounded his studio with Lijia Lu in 1993, merging private spatial experimentation with extensive academic leadership at MIT, Peking University, and the Pritzker Architecture Prize jury. Key works like the Liangzhu Campus for the China Academy of Art, ChunYangTai Arts and Cultural Centre, and Maison de la Chine demonstrate his commitment to joining regional heritage with international architectural logic.

Awarded the DFA Design Leadership Award (DLA), Sonia Cheng proves how mathematical rigor can shape intuitive, atmosphere-driven spaces. Leading both Rosewood Hotel Group and Chow Tai Fook Jewellery Group, the Harvard-educated executive approaches built environments with analytical precision. Since 2011, she has expanded Rosewood to more than 50 locations worldwide, anchoring each property in site-specific craft and local art, while steering Chow Tai Fook through a fresh era of international retail.

The DFA World’s Outstanding Chinese Designer (WOCD) title goes to Hong Kong artist Wallace Chan, recognizing five decades of radical innovation across sculpture and jewelry art. Completely self-taught, Chan merged Chinese philosophy with scientific experimentation, pioneering the three-dimensional Wallace Cut in 1987, specialized clawless settings, and structural titanium sculpture. He expanded his repertoire with Wallace Chan Porcelain, a specialized compound significantly stronger than structural steel. With major acquisitions across the Victoria and Albert Museum and the British Museum, his practice turns esoteric concepts into palpable, light-bending structures.

Named DFA Designer of the Year (DOY), Vector Architects founder Dong Gong has established a compelling spatial language shaped by natural light, local climate, and tectonic clarity. A foreign member of the French Academy of Architecture, Gong transforms everyday landscapes into contemplative civic encounters. His defining works, including the coastal Seashore Library, the Seashore Chapel, the Yangshuo Sugar House hotel conversion, and the Jingyang Camphor Court, showcase an agile balance of raw materiality and site history. With major presentations at MoMA in New York and the Venice Biennale, his practice stands among the most resonant voices in contemporary Asian architecture.

Closing the roster of honorees, the DFA Asian Design Vanguard (ADV) award spotlights Tianyuan Li for recalibrating the contours of electric mobility. Currently heading design at Xiaomi Auto, Li arrived on the global stage as the first Chinese car designer based at BMW headquarters in Munich, steering exterior form on forward-looking projects like the BMW iX and the circular economy concept BMW i Vision Circular. At Xiaomi Auto, he translates digital operating systems into tactile aerodynamic silhouettes, establishing a fluid aesthetic across the Xiaomi SU7 electric sedan, the Xiaomi YU7, and concepts such as the Xiaomi SkyNomad and Xiaomi Vision Gran Turismo. His work demonstrates how vehicle architecture can bridge consumer electronics with high-speed engineering.

Spatial Design takes the lead as the Hong Kong Design Centre announces the 209 winning projects of the DFA Design for Asia Awards 2026. Chosen from entries across 15 economies by a 26-member jury of local and international design figures, the selection spans six design disciplines, with Spatial Design recording the highest proportion of winning entries. The 2026 edition also sees Grand Award winners from Thailand and India return to the top leaderboard for the first time since 2020, pointing to the growing influence of ASEAN design studios.

#8996. BIG reveals "modular blueprint" for Refugee City in Uganda

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled plans for Refugee City, a masterplan that reimagines the Bidi Bidi refugee settlement in Uganda as an economic hub.

Developed by BIG in collaboration with social enterprise To.org, the masterplan proposes essential civic infrastructure such as housing, schools and markets for the largest refugee settlement in Africa, home to around 250,000 displaced people.

The initiative was conceptualised as an alternative to short-term aid and charity-led approaches to refugee settlements, providing a “resilient economic model” that empowers displaced communities.

“If the average stay in refugee camps is around two decades, then the term temporary cannot be said to suffice,” said studio founder Bjarke Ingels.

“If we start thinking of cities rather than camps, then charity becomes investments into the future, and if companies can be incentivised to locate their production in refugee cities, then the refugees can be given economic opportunities that they currently long for.”

If completed, the project would sit alongside an existing performing arts centre completed on the site in 2024.

The masterplan is designed by BIG to be “scalable and modular” to facilitate its implementation in other locations.

“We have attempted to design a scalable, phaseable, modular blueprint for a new way to accommodate the global flow of refugees,” Ingels said.

In a bid to allow the city to grow organically, the proposal takes a “fractal approach” – beginning with the establishment of housing units before expanding to neighbourhoods and eventually districts over several years.

The first phase of the project comprises a prototype single-family housing unit, which is currently being built on the site. Its modular structure was designed to improve existing shelter typologies, while also drawing on local buildings.

Once complete, the unit will function as an operational guesthouse to accommodate international investors and future collaborators on the site.

“The prototype base unit is inspired by local vernacular settlements where homes grow as a sequence of rooms around shared spaces,” To.org co-founder Nachson Mimran told Dezeen.

Renders of the city reveal designs for a commercial street lined with markets and built from local materials such as brick and bamboo.

The Bidi Bidi settlement in Uganda was chosen as the site for the inaugural Refugee City because of the country’s 2006 Refugee Act, which grants refugees the right to work and start businesses, freedom of movement, and to acquire agricultural plots within integrated rural settlements.

“There are very few nations offering this unique combination which makes Uganda the ideal location for the inaugural Refugee City,” Mimran said.

The realisation of the full-scale masterplan in Bidi Bidi is dependent on capital investment, while any future initiatives will require host-nation governments to be willing to grant flexibility and legal work rights to refugees.

#8995. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#8994. 6 Supplements Doctors Actually Take

These days, it seems like everyone is taking a supplement—to look better, think better, sleep better, relax better, poop better, or work out better. And you’re not imagining things: Half of adults and one-third of children in the United States take supplements regularly, according to the Office of Dietary Supplements.

Supplements may be ubiquitous, but many experts have serious reservations about their rise. First, most physicians recommend obtaining nutrients directly from food rather than a pill or capsule. Second, supplements aren’t reviewed for safety and effectiveness by the FDA before they hit shelves. Because of all the concerns surrounding supplements, Jeffrey Linder, MD, MPH, a general internist and professor of medicine at the Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine, takes a dim view of the category overall: In fact, “a vast majority of supplements are probably worthless,” he tells SELF.

Still, there are exceptions to every rule—and supplements are no different. Many experts, as it turns out, do take some type of supplement, but they are choosy about which ones they select. Read on to learn more about six they actually use.

How it works: Vitamin D plays key roles in bone health and immune function. In fact, low vitamin D is associated with a wide swath of medical conditions, according to Dr. Linder—including cancer, autoimmune diseases, infectious diseases, and cardiovascular issues (and, famously, seasonal affective disorder, or SAD).

Why some docs like it: Vitamin D deficiency is widespread, especially among people who live at northern latitudes that don’t see as much sun during the winter, and people with darker skin. What’s more, few foods contain significant amounts of vitamin D, so it’s tough to source enough from your diet. Lawrence Green, MD, a dermatologist and clinical professor at the George Washington University School of Medicine and Health Sciences, tells SELF that these two factors make vitamin D a rare nutrient “we do need to take supplements for.” Nearly every single one of the eight doctors who spoke with SELF for this article said they take a vitamin D supplement, especially in the winter, though the frequency and dosage varied.

What to keep in mind: Most docs recommend vitamin D3 (also known as cholecalciferol) over vitamin D2 (also known as ergocalciferol), as studies have shown that D3 is more effective at raising vitamin D levels in your blood. Whichever option you decide on, try to take it with food—specifically, an item that contains fat. Because vitamin D is a fat-soluble nutrient, it “absorbs better that way,” Sara Velayati, MD, an obesity medicine specialist at Montefiore Einstein and an assistant professor at Albert Einstein College of Medicine in New York City, tells SELF. For this reason, Dr. Green makes a point of taking his supplements with breakfast or dinner. “The fattier and thicker the meal,” the better, he says.

What it does: Calcium is a mineral that helps build and maintain strong bones and teeth. Women in their 40s approaching menopausal age should make it a particular priority to ensure their intake is adequate, Rachel Pessah-Pollack, MD, an endocrinologist at NYU Langone Health and a clinical professor at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, tells SELF, as the physical changes that come with perimenopause and menopause can heighten bone loss and downstream health conditions like osteoporosis.

Who takes it: Like the other supplements on this list, calcium is best sourced from your diet, Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. “But if you’re not able to (I try to get dairy products but often come up short), a supplement is needed.” She takes a combined calcium and vitamin D tablet daily, as vitamin D helps calcium absorb.

How to take it: “The type of calcium supplements you are taking matters,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium carbonate and calcium citrate are the two most common. “Calcium carbonate should be taken with food because it requires gastric acid to be absorbed,” Dr. Pessah-Pollack says. Calcium citrate is an alternative that can be taken with or without food.

How it works: Magnesium is a mineral that can enhance sleep and muscle recovery. Research has also shown that it’s effective at preventing migraines, Raquel Zemtsov, MD, MPH, a family medicine doctor and assistant professor at the University of Pittsburgh School of Medicine, tells SELF.

Why some docs like it: In addition to Dr. Zemtsov, who takes magnesium to stave off migraine symptoms, Dr. Velayati takes magnesium for the sleep benefits. Likewise, Sheeva Talebian, MD, a reproductive endocrinologist at CCRM Fertility of New York, and Kathleen Jordan, MD, an internal medicine physician and chief medical officer at Midi Health, also turn to it at bedtime to boost their shut-eye.

What to keep in mind: Some types of magnesium are better tolerated, says Dr. Velayati—something to note if you’re especially sensitive to side effects. Magnesium glycinate “avoids the gastrointestinal upset caused by magnesium oxides and magnesium citrates,” for example, Dr. Jordan says. Depending on your needs, however, magnesium glycinate might not be the best option: Magnesium oxide is the recommended magnesium type for migraines, so that’s the one Dr. Zemtsov keeps on hand, for example. Taking magnesium with food can also help prevent GI distress, according to Dr. Velayati.

How it works: Omega-3 fatty acids are polyunsaturated fats that are important for cardiovascular health. Common omega-3 supplements include fish oil and krill oil.

Why some docs like it: Dr. Jordan, Dr. Talebian, and Dr. Velayati all take omega-3s. “With their anti-inflammatory properties and association with improved brain health, this is a popular supplement among physicians, myself included,” Dr. Jordan, who takes krill oil, says. Similarly, Dr. Velayati dabbles in fish oil, but takes it selectively. “The right dose really depends on the goal, but I don’t think it’s necessary for everyone,” she says.

What to keep in mind: Fish oil supplements can have a characteristic fishy aftertaste, so it might take some trial and error to find one that works for you (read: doesn’t leave you gagging). What’s more, absorption and bioavailability can be a challenge, according to Dr. Jordan. Because omega-3s, like vitamin D, are fat-soluble, taking fish oil with a meal that contains fat can help skirt this problem. Some claim krill oil doesn’t cause the dreaded aftertaste as much as fish oil, and evidence suggests it’s also better absorbed by the body.

How it works: Iron, a mineral, acts as an essential ingredient in hemoglobin, a protein found in your red blood cells. Without enough iron, your blood won’t be able to carry out its core task of delivering oxygen to organs and tissues, resulting in anemia.

Why some docs like it: Iron deficiency is common in women due to the loss of blood during menstruation every month. “Occasionally, despite trying my hardest to seek out iron-rich foods, I still develop an iron deficiency,” Dr. Zemtsov says. When that happens, she takes ferrous gluconate (a particular type of iron supplement) every other day to treat or prevent anemia, since research shows iron supplements are better absorbed and cause fewer side effects that way. Dr. Jordan also takes iron supplements, citing the advantages for sleep, hair health, and overall energy.

What to keep in mind: Iron absorption is enhanced by vitamin C, so pairing your iron supplement with a food that contains vitamin C or even a vitamin C supplement—as Dr. Zemtsov does—can be helpful.

How it works: Fiber, a type of carb, boosts digestion in a variety of ways: It keeps you full, helps prevent constipation, and supports bowel health. Besides the GI stuff, it also serves other functions in your body, including stabilizing your blood sugar and lowering “bad” LDL cholesterol.

Why some docs like it: “Unless you are that rare woman who regularly gets in her 25 to 30 grams per day, extra fiber intake is beneficial for almost everyone, and addresses multiple issues for me personally, including prediabetes and a rising cholesterol level,” Dr. Jordan says. She takes a fiber supplement as needed, on days when she doesn’t manage to hit her goal.

What to keep in mind: If your body isn’t acclimated to a high fiber intake, suddenly bombarding it could cause some digestive distress (think gas and bloating), so start slow to ease the transition. You’ll also need to increase your water intake simultaneously, since fiber requires water to work.

“When someone is considering a supplement, I usually recommend having a specific reason for taking it”—like a confirmed nutritional deficiency, Dr. Velayati says. “Overall, I view supplements as a way to fill a gap, not a substitute for good nutrition, sleep, exercise, and evidence-based medical care.” The bottom line: Supplements are really meant for plugging holes in your diet.

#8993. Polestar Formula 2030 concept car "screams performance"

Swedish electric-vehicle brand Polestar has unveiled the Formula 2030 concept car featuring interchangeable, customisable dashboard buttons.

The first Polestar concept created under the direction of head of design Philipp Römers, the Formula 2030 is intended to herald the design direction of the company’s production cars in the coming years.

It takes the form of a low-slung sports car with proportions that Römers said “scream performance”.

With signature “Dual Blade” headlights, the front of the car previews the face of the next-generation Polestar 2, a saloon scheduled to launch in 2027.

Meanwhile, the tail of the Formula 2030 mirrors the upcoming Polestar 7 crossover SUV, moving away from the continuous rear lightbar that has become widespread among electric cars in favour of separate “Single Blade” lights.

Unlike Polestar’s most recently released production vehicles, the Polestar 4 and Polestar 5, the Formula 2030 also has a conventional rear windscreen.

“Design should always reflect the values and mission of a brand and that is exactly what we did with Polestar Formula 2030 concept,” said Römers, who joined Polestar from Audi in January 2025.

“It is a physical embodiment of how we apply Polestar’s core values of design, performance and sustainability to the next production cars.”

At 1.35 metres tall, 4.68 metres long and 2.02 metres wide, the Formula 2030 has a very low roofline but a broad stance.

Its styling was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and substantial 22-inch wheels.

Other sporty design elements include a deep front splitter and a single vertical windscreen wiper.

The Formula 2030 showcases a newly developed paint colour called Nitrogen, with accents of gold dotted throughout the car.

Inside, the design echoes efforts in recent concept cars from other carmakers to emphasise the driving experience.

The cockpit features a curved screen band mounted above the steering wheel, presenting information to the driver.

Another screen is integrated into the centre console, which slopes gently up to the dashboard.

A sliding “drive mode selector” on the centre console would allow the car to alternate between three modes – Performance, Normal and Autonomous – changing the angle of the central screen, seating and steering wheel to allow for a more passive or active driving position.

The Formula 2030 embraces a wider trend in car design back towards incorporating physical buttons, rather than only touchscreens.

Also occupying the central console is an interface of eight large mechanical controls. These can be configured to the user’s preferences, with choices between different types of buttons and switches capable of being programmed for specific functions.

In a modest nod to sustainability, the seat backs are made from a bio-based composite combining European flax and bio-based polypropylene, while the insides of the doors are made from a single material in order to be recyclable.

Headquartered in Gothenburg, Polestar has emphasised design and sustainability since it was spun out of Volvo as a premium EV brand in 2017.

Amid heavy financial losses, it has increased its production of SUVs, which tend to be popular with consumers and deliver higher profit margins. SUVs or SUV-adjacent cars now account for three of the five models in its lineup.

SUVs are often associated with a greater environmental impact than other types of cars, but Polestar denies watering down its ambitions on sustainability.

According to its most recent sustainability report, published in April, the company is ahead of schedule on a target to halve greenhouse-gas emissions per vehicle sold between 2020 and 2030.

It is the only car brand that publishes life-cycle carbon assessments for all its models. Assessments for the upcoming Polestar 2 and Polestar 7 have not yet been calculated.

“Learnings from the cars we have already produced will be channelled into the new cars to bring the CO2e figures in as low as possible,” a spokesperson told Dezeen.

In 2021, Polestar announced a project to produce a “truly climate-neutral car” by 2030. Earlier this year, it pushed this target back to 2035 owing to the “scale and complexity of the challenge”.

Other concept cars recently covered on Dezeen include the flying Tesla Roadster and a Fiat that transforms from an SUV into a pickup truck.

#8992. Are Single Older Ladies Really Happy Without Marriage? Experts Weigh In

At some point in most women’s lives, a familiar line of thinking creeps in—whether on its own or planted by well-meaning parents: What if I don’t get married? What if I never find my person and end up alone?

For Joan, the panic hit in her 30s—strong enough to land her in a psychologist’s office. Back then, she says, “a woman who didn’t want a husband was assumed to have something wrong with her.” But her therapist—married with children, yet more open-minded than most—didn’t try to correct her with cheesy motivational mantras or fear tactics about a “ticking clock.” Instead, she asked a different question: What kind of husband would you want, if you had one?

Joan listed a few traits. Someone busy, she recalls saying. Someone deeply absorbed in his own life—his job, his hobbies, his community.

“So you'd want someone intellectually stimulating?” her therapist asked.

“No,” Joan replied. “I’d want someone who’s never home.”

It landed as a joke, though deep down, it wasn’t. What came from that session was an almost accidental realization that sounded radical at the time (it was around 1980): “Some people genuinely live their best lives independently,” Joan tells me. Now 79, single, and uninterested in changing her relationship status, she has spent decades proving her theory true.

For much of modern history, women like Joan were cast as anomalies, freaks, or worse: cautionary tales. There’s “the childless cat lady.” The “old maid.” The “lonely spinster.” Singlehood was framed as a transitional phase, a temporary stop on the way to finding the One. Not an end goal, and certainly not a fulfilling one.

But the stigma is softening—and the older, unmarried women of this generation are living proof that a life without a husband isn’t a fallback; it’s a deeply satisfying choice.

You can see it in the collective fatigue around modern dating (78% of users on apps including Tinder, Hinge, and Bumble reported feeling burnt out, per a recent Forbes Health survey). Young adults in their mid 20s to early 30s (the supposed “prime marriage years”) are having far less sex than previous generations, with sexual inactivity up roughly 50% for women over the past decade. The shift shows up in pop culture too—in particular, the growing appetite for plots that sideline romance in favor of friendship, independence, and chosen families (like in Barbie and Wicked).

But perhaps the clearest proof is in lived experiences. The several 70-somethings I spoke with for this story have been single for decades—and aren’t wishing they’d done it any differently. If anything, their lives carry a sense of ease and expansiveness. Many describe weekly, laughter-filled girls’ nights and happy hours; solo trips planned on a whim; financial freedom to buy property, adopt pets, start small businesses…literally do whatever they want, whenever they want. A few still date casually, dipping in and out of steamy flings only when it suits them. Others have opted out of romance entirely. “My favorite part?” one 73-year-old woman tells me bluntly. “Not having to bicker or put up with an incompetent man. That’s probably why I’m the least stressed I’ve ever been.”

Across their stories, there’s no regret or hint of “missing out.” Just single older ladies enjoying where they are—nothing like the caricatures of the bitter man-hater or the desperate, unlucky romantic we’re used to seeing.

As Joan is quick to point out, “not everyone starts off wanting a romantic relationship and then moves on to singlehood as Plan B.” It’s a perspective that’s become increasingly common, so much so that sociologist Bella DePaulo, PhD, built a framework (and wrote a book) about it: being Single at Heart. These are women (including herself) who don’t end up alone; they orient toward it as a genuine preference.

“I still smile when I think about the men I dated when I was a very young adult,” Dr. DePaulo, 72, tells me. “But I remember even more fondly how I felt when each of those relationships ended: finally free.”

The practical benefits of singledom—solitude, strong friendships, fewer relational stressors—aren’t exclusive to unmarried folks. “But in my opinion, couples are never free the way single people are,” Dr. DePaulo says. The difference, she claims, is psychological: the ability to structure a day, a life, or a passing thought without reflexively factoring in another person’s needs or reactions. “A romantic partner is also there in your mind almost all the time,” Dr. DePaulo points out—even if only on the periphery. “That might be comforting for some. But it can also feel a bit unwelcome, as if they’re always considering what their significant other may be wanting or feeling.” Remove that, and your attention and energy become fully your own.

Of course, the ability to choose this lifestyle is relatively recent. For centuries, marriage wasn’t just a matter of romance—women relied on it for financial stability, social acceptance, and a sanctioned path to family, Kris Marsh, PhD, sociologist and author of The Love Jones Cohort: Single and Living Alone in the Black Middle Class, tells SELF. But with greater access to education, careers, and economic independence (along with broader definitions of intimacy, family, and fulfillment), the pressure to couple up has eased. As of 2023, 42% of US adults were unpartnered, according to the Pew Research Center (up from 29% in 1990). And among the non-daters younger than 50, half aren’t interested in a relationship—though enjoying your single status doesn’t have to involve an anti-love attitude.

“Now, a lot of women are looking for something additive,” Dr. Marsh says. “I’ve heard over and over, ‘I’m already in a very good place on my own. So you can’t be a distraction. You can’t disrupt my peace.’” Though for most, that epiphany doesn’t happen overnight.

Alice Foster, who recently turned 80, is a classic example of someone who followed the cultural script handed to many in her generation: marry young, raise children, enjoy the stability. “It was fine, but I felt like it was never really about me,” Foster tells SELF. “It wasn’t my life.”

In 1988, her marriage ended in divorce—though what followed wasn’t the loss she had been taught to fear. It was space. Peace. Recalibration. She moved upstate. Went back to school. Built a new career in nursing. Slowly, she began constructing a life that finally felt like her own.

“I feel like I’m in my 50s. It’s been so fun,” she reflects. “I love being retired. I love traveling. I love having people visit me. I love not having to answer to anybody. I’ve been single for so long and loving this life so much that, honestly, I don’t want to get tied down.” And that, experts say, is often how it works.

Rather than being a fixed moral stance or a lifelong rejection of romance, singlehood tends to be a lived, flexible experience—an acceptance of being on your own that you don’t always realize you’re choosing until later. Maybe, like Foster, you leave an unsatisfying marriage. You pull back on exhaustive online dating. You decide this is the year you’ll focus on work, hobbies, or travel. Over time, you stop planning life around the possibility of a relationship…and start seeing that you already have the joy you thought only a husband could provide.

Still, a question tends to linger: Are these women actually happy?

Recent research suggests yes—in fact, satisfaction with singlehood tends to increase with age, starting for people in their 40s. Despite cultural progress, there’s still skepticism as to why anyone would willingly stay single. Whereas married people are taken at their word when they claim fulfillment (even though we know that’s not always true), those who deviate face public scrutiny. “They have to be extra strong, exceptionally confident to stand comfortably in their singleness and validate to the world that they are, in fact, thriving,” Dr. Marsh adds—an expectation that flattens single older ladies into either a hyper-independent success story or a pitiable failure, with little room for nuance.

But that pressure can have an unintended effect too. After decades of being asked by society to justify their lifestyle, many simply stop performing. All of the women I spoke with didn’t overexplain. They weren’t defensive. They didn’t seem especially interested in winning me over.

It takes a certain kind of confidence and clarity to stop shaping your life around what’s expected and historically rewarded, and instead follow what feels good, without apology. What you get then, as Dr. Marsh has observed in her research, is a quieter, rarer form of happiness—one that isn’t performed and doesn’t ask for external validation. Instead, it feels much more genuine. It endures.

#8991. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8990. john pawson sets white ribbon staircase against 18th century baroque portal at the madrid EDITION

ian schrager pairs john pawson’s refined minimalism with françois champsaur’s artistry inside madrid’s former monte de piedad bank, converted by OAB and ruiz-larrea into the hotel brand's second spanish address.

sofia lekka angelopoulou November 17, 2026 6 min

John Pawson takes his cue at The Madrid EDITION hotel from an eighteenth-century baroque portal he inherited. Spanish architect Pedro de Ribera carved it for the chapel of the Monte de Piedad, the charitable pawnshop that Francisco Piquer, chaplain of the Descalzas Reales convent across the square, founded in 1702 to lend to the poor. The savings bank that grew out of that pawnshop demolished the chapel in the 1960s and kept the portal, resetting it on the face of its new office building.

It is this building that OAB (Office of Architecture in Barcelona) and Ruiz-Larrea convert into the brand’s second Spanish address after the Barcelona EDITION of 2018, with interiors by Pawson and Paris-based François Champsaur, all orchestrated under the eye of Ian Schrager. Pawson names the challenges of the inherited architecture as the project’s defining inspiration, and his response turns on a lobby with two very different entry experiences: a lower entrance clad in dark baroque timber around a sculptural white staircase, and a second entrance through the portal itself on the historic Plaza de las Descalzas.

From the historic square, the Madrid EDITION building reads as clean-lined and almost reticent, its single flourish the carved decorative portal that frames the entrance. Around the corner, a copper canopy and a curtain of greenery announce the main entry, with Pawson’s white sculptural spiral staircase, free of visible handrails, coiling up toward the lobby where the two entrances meet.

There, the Lobby Bar sits beneath an undulating plane that softens the room’s proportions, lit almost entirely indirectly, with spotlights reserved for the pieces worth looking at: reissued Jean-Michel Frank sofas and armchairs, recycled bronze stools cast by Maison Intègre at its foundry in Ouagadougou, rope-wrapped chairs by Christian Astuguevieille, and a pool table that Emmanuel Levet Stenne cut from a single slab of white Bianco Neve marble. A hand-scalloped copper bar runs along one side with a backlit caged bottle display behind it, and a U-shaped sofa with backlit shelves anchors the middle of the room.

In a corner off the lobby, the Punch Room goes darker still, with dark oak panels, a basalt stone fireplace, gray pony hair armchairs, a brushed copper bar and a bronze-polished mirror by Paris studio Garnier & Linker.

Ribera’s carving does not stay outside, it reappears in the double-height dining room of the all-day Italian restaurant, which enters directly through the portal from the plaza. There, dark oak wall panels take their pattern from the stonework a few meters away, hung with two alabaster and plaster pendants by Levet Stenne. The room opens into a lounge along a long green marble bar laid over white oak floors, then into a lighter third area of white marble tables.

The motif travels upstairs too, in each of the hotel’s 200 guest rooms, where custom made plaster headboards are shaped after the elaborate form of the hotel’s baroque portal. The rooms’ interiors carry the contrast of light and darkness down to the threshold. An entrance panelled in dark oak gives onto a light-filled palette of whites and creams, with custom furnishings and the natural textures of linen, limestone and timber forming what the hotel calls an honest and discreet canvas for the detail work.

‘I am very proud of this project,’ says Schrager, the visionary pioneer of the boutique and lifestyle hotel brand. ‘Not a single detail has been overlooked and the finished product has created a unique and magical concept.’

23 of the 200 rooms are suites, while two penthouses take the west side of the fourth floor for the sunset, arranged as duplexes with the bedrooms upstairs and the living space and a butler’s kitchen below. The larger of them, the Madrid Penthouse, opens onto a panoramic terrace with its own infinity pool set in greenery, furnished with a leather and wood daybed by BassamFellows and an eight-seat travertine dining table on lacquered metal feet.

The fourth-floor rooftop holds the property’s showpiece: the largest infinity pool built on the roof of an existing building in Madrid, edged by 25 sunbeds and five cabanas, with the city’s terracotta rooftops unrolling toward the sunset. The rooftop is also home to Oroya, the Peruvian restaurant of chef Diego Muñoz, set in a greenhouse-like dining room of blackened steel, climbing plants and colored glass. Outside, a vine-covered pergola shades the restaurant’s terrace, where a fireplace, a bleached teak bar and a long oak table offer guests a relaxed, convivial atmosphere to enjoy lazy lunches or afternoon cocktails.

#8989. Perforated brick walls envelop giant market in Kinshasa by Think Tank Architecture

Photography by Martin Argyroglo excluding top photo by Ville Kinshasa & SZTC

French studio Think Tank Architecture has created a market in the capital of the Democratic Republic of Congo, with space for 20,000 vendors across its geometric brick-and-concrete structure.

Named Zando Central Market, the building replaces a historic market on the same site in Kinshasa that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

Think Tank Architecture was brought in to design the replacement market after the original building had already been torn down. The studio used this as an opportunity to completely reimagine the role and function of the market, while taking visual cues from the original building and others like it in the city.

Alongside an increased number of vendor stalls, the 82,000-square-metre replacement incorporates storage space, a fire station, a police station, a medical centre, a vet’s, offices and a food court.

“The new market is on the same site as the ancient one, on the 3.7-hectare plot,” Think Tank Architecture told Dezeen.

“However, the building’s footprint has been totally redefined, taking into consideration the scale of the program and the urban context,” it continued.

“We wanted it to be an African market, and not an interpretation of it. Our comprehension comes from academic, historic and architectural research, dialogue with the client and then visits to other markets in Kinshasa.”

Zando Central Market has a rectangular plan measuring 245 metres in length and 150 metres in width. It contains 650 shops with space for 20,000 vendors, which is “more than 5 times its original capacity”, according to the studio.

At its heart is the central covered market, spanning two double-height levels, with three large entrances and outward views used to orient visitors.

It is surrounded by a three-storey building containing the other facilities. Landscaped patios punctuate the plan, carving out space for public squares and informal markets to take place.

“It’s an important part of our approach to keep the building open to the public, including the more modest,” said Think Tank Architecture.

The material palette for the project comprises brick and concrete, chosen to be in keeping with the local context and skills of the region’s construction workers. Demolition waste from the original market was used in the substructure.

“We are quite happy to say that this project reactivated three terracotta factories within a 60-kilometre distance from the market,” reflected the studio.

It uses a mushroom-slab structural system, in which the columns flare at their top, referencing the original market’s design.

Meanwhile, the perforated brick facades were designed to facilitate natural ventilation and provide shade from the sun.

In tandem with the thermal mass from the concrete, this helps cool the building, minimising the need for technical cooling equipment and keeping project costs low.

Interior finishes were also kept deliberately simple for cost reasons. However, the perforations of the facades help add flourish, evoking moucharabiehs – a type of projecting oriel window enclosed with wooden latticework, typically seen in traditional Islamic architecture.

Zando Central Market is on the eight-strong shortlist for the civic project category of the 2026 Dezeen Awards, alongside projects including Sydney Fish Market by 3XN and TCC DAKA Renewable Resource Recycling Center by KPF.

It is yet to officially open, as the second phase of the project – involving the renovation of the surrounding streets – needs to be completed to allow access.

“This phase of works is under the city’s supervision and is going slower,” said Think Tank Architecture. “We hope, and it’s in our client’s interest, that the market will be able to open by the end of this year.”

Other market architecture recently featured on Dezeen includes the multi-level Tepoztlán Market in central Mexico by local studios Ramírez Suarez Arquitectos and Laboratorio Regional de Arquitectura, and an open-air market in Colombia designed by Tarq Studio to accommodate community gatherings.

#8988. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8987. First Ferrari Style flagship store in New York features metallic facade

Photography courtesy Ferrari Style

Architecture studios Gonzalez Haase AAS and Formafantasma have worked with Ferrari Style creative director Rocco Iannone on the brand’s first permanent store in New York, clad in a metallic facade.

Located in Manhattan’s SoHo neighbourhood, the flagship store for Ferrari’s fashion label is in a long, narrow building at the corner of Prince Street and Mercer Street and spreads across two levels.

Berlin-based Gonzalez Haase AAS clad the building in brushed metal, with curved window mullions covering floor-to-ceiling glass along its length.

Under Iannone, the team referenced the Ferrari Officina concept, a central theme of the brand that seeks to connect fashion and automotive. It considers “the workshop as a junction at which artistic instinct, scientific rigour, craftsmanship and mechanical precision converge,” according to the team.

“The Officina is the place where intuition is given form through discipline, and where the human touch works in harmony with mechanical precision,” said Iannone.

The opening follows another Ferrari Style store opened earlier this year in London, designed by the same team, and both stores share pops of red, warm beige finishes, and steel accents.

However, the New York space was designed to fit in with the city. The team said the New York location reflects the “form, scale and material character of SoHo”.

“For New York, we wanted to translate this spirit into a space in which architecture, fashion and object design each retain their own identity while contributing to a single Ferrari language,” said the team.

“Every material and detail has been chosen to express this balance between art and science, creating an environment that is open, evolving and in direct dialogue with the energy of SoHo.”

Men’s ready-to-wear is located on the first floor, with objects displayed on units designed by Formafantasma.

The space is bordered by a deep red curtain and large rectangular ceiling lights.

A staircase to the left side of the store leads to the “more intimate” second level, containing women’s ready-to-wear, footwear and accessories collections.

It also contains the store’s atelier, the second worldwide apart from the London location.

Wrapped in leather curtains, the space provides a private setting for personalisations and alterations. A table containing samples of textiles and hardware sits at the centre.

Ferrari Style, the brand’s luxury fashion line founded in 2021, has other US locations in New Jersey, Miami, and Las Vegas.

Ferrari recently unveiled a laptop collaboration with HP, as well as its first electric vehicle earlier this year.

#8986. 5 Signs You’re in a One-Sided Friendship, According to Experts

Welcome to Asking for a Friend, a weekly series dedicated to solving the messy, awkward, and confusing parts of modern friendship. Because truth is, our platonic relationships are often the most complicated. Send us your friendship dilemmas here, and we might feature one in a future column.

Most friendships will never be truly 50/50, but at the very least they run on an unspoken agreement: both people show up, reach out, and add some fuel to the tank that keeps the engine going. If that balance consistently feels off—not just once or twice, but over the course of weeks or months—it’s hard not to wonder whether something deeper is going on.

You might notice in small but telling ways: Looking back at your messages, it dawns on you that you’re initiating every conversation. They call, if at all, only when they’re bored or when it’s convenient. And then there’s the sharper sting of noticing how effortlessly they find time for other people—just not for you (a surprisingly common frustration you can read more about here).

To be fair, life can get in the way—people get busy, schedules clash, and our friends can’t always be as available as we’d like—but that doesn’t make it any less frustrating or stop you from feeling resentful when you’re waiting days for a simple “How are you?” But how do you know if this is a temporary lapse or a more unhealthy one-sided friendship? Here are the biggest red flags therapists want you to watch out for.

Look through your texts and DMs: Are you always the first to send a message? When’s the last time they suggested hanging out? You can also experiment by not reaching out to see how long it takes for them to initiate contact. If weeks (or months) go by without a word, their silence may indicate who’s really holding this connection together.

“At a minimum, a good friend (even a busy one) will periodically check in out of curiosity and interest,” Tiana Leeds, LMFT, a therapist based in Santa Barbara, California, tells SELF. After all, someone who truly cares about you should want to know what’s going on in your life, which is why if they consistently don’t try to get in touch (or only expect you to do so), they may not be genuinely interested in your world.

Venting to your friends is natural—some would even argue it can strengthen your bond. That said, being there for each other is supposed to be a two-way street, Hope Kelaher, LCSW, author of Here to Make Friends: How to Make Friends as an Adult, tells SELF.

If someone unloads their laundry list of problems but doesn’t listen to yours, “they’re likely using you as their on-call therapist,” Kelaher says. This one-directional dynamic could look like a person who constantly complains about their boss but changes the subject whenever you open up about your work-related stress. Or they dominate dinner conversations with their dating disasters, yet they’re “busy,” uninterested, or MIA when you need relationship advice. Over time, investing all your time and energy into people who won’t give back can drain your energy, Leeds says, and leave you feeling neglected by a person who’s supposed to have your back.

Maybe they insist on eating at restaurants near their place, which means you have to travel across town every single time. They only reach out when “better” plans fall through (“Hey, my dinner got canceled. What are you doing tonight?”), making you feel more like an afterthought than a priority. More subtly, perhaps they’re only interested in brief 15-minute coffee chats that fit their schedule instead of a dedicated dinner or movie night.

“In a healthy relationship there should always be a give-and-take,” Kelaher says, meaning both people need to compromise. So it’s disheartening when, again and again, someone you’d do anything for won’t meet you halfway (sometimes literally).

Your friend might be a workaholic or chronically forgetful (which, don’t get us wrong, is still frustrating). But that alone doesn’t mean your bond is one-sided.

Instead, “consider the bigger picture and ask yourself, ‘Is their behavior a reflection of not caring about me, or just a difference in availability and communication style?’” Leeds says. As an example, someone who takes five business days to reply to anyone’s messages may not be singling you out. What’s more telling, though, is if that same person who’s “too swamped” to text you regularly posts Instagram stories of brunches, dinners, and post-work meetups with others in their social circle. Or if your usually punctual friend (who’s known for being reliable) is comfortable canceling plans only with you. These inconsistencies, Kelaher says, suggest that they’re perfectly capable of showing up—just not for you.

Let’s say you mentioned how important it would be to have support at your first 5K race. A friend who truly cares might surprise you at the finish line with flowers, or at the very least shoot over a heartfelt “Good luck!” or “Congrats!” In a one-sided friendship, however, this kind of consideration may be missing entirely. They might downplay your achievement (“Sorry I couldn’t make it, but it was such a short race!”) or forget your big day without a hint of apology.

True friends go the extra mile to celebrate your successes and be there during tough moments. That’s why if someone repeatedly forgets significant events like your birthday, or rarely shows empathy for your challenges (like a scary medical procedure, a high-stakes presentation), they may not be as invested as they should be.

Therapists recommended bringing up your concerns non-confrontationally.

Ideally, their response can give you a glimpse into whether they’re aware of this imbalance and, more importantly, if they’re willing to work on it. That said, you can’t force someone to be a good friend, so if they don’t care enough to show up for you, know that you deserve better. “After all, friendships take work, Leeds says. “But it’s not meant to be done by just one person.”
