#8919. Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year revealed

A tree-top sauna that punctures its architectural framework with the surrounding woodland has been named Dezeen Awards 2026 architecture project of the year following the announcement of all 19 architecture category winners at a party in London.

The 19 winners awarded at the ninth annual Dezeen Awards ceremony are located in 11 different countries, including Canada, France, India, Japan and Mexico.

Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna won the project of the year award in the architecture sector, it was also named leisure and wellness project of the year.

Leisure and wellness projects win big again

The judges hailed the biophilic project as “beautifully minimalist with a spiritual touch of the soul”.

“It’s totally fresh, totally innovative, and never seen before,” they added.

The win marks the second consecutive year that the leisure and wellness project of the year has gone on to claim the overall sector title, following Herzog & de Meuron’s win last year.

The winning project of the year was up against category winners including a sprawling brick-clad university building modelled on stepped wells in India, a country house with walls formed of unstabilised rammed earth in the UK and a project featuring an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through in Mexico.

A housing project that appears as if emerging from the natural landscape and a viewpoint designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the burial site of a legendary Viking were also amongst the category winners.

Read more about all the winning architecture projects below:

Architecture project of the year and leisure and wellness project of the year: Daichi Silent River Tree Sauna by Daichi

The project is nestled within a forest in Kanagawa, southwest of Tokyo, and forms part of the Daichi Silent River retreat alongside guest cabins and additional sauna spaces.

Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly

The idea for the project was to make the trees feel part of the architecture, using them as both supports and the defining feature of the pared-back structure.

“Leisure and wellness is also about mental health, which this project addresses perfectly,” said the master jury.

“It is a building that offers a spiritual connection between humans and nature.”

House (urban) project of the year: Amami House by Sakai Architects

Local studio Sakai Architects won urban house of the year for its off-grid home on Amami Ōshima, an island in the Amami archipelago off Japan‘s southern coast.

This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature

The design was informed by the region’s traditional materials and crafts and its development was spurred by the increase in extreme weather conditions on the island.

“This house shows how we can live sustainably on a small footprint, in close relationship to nature,” the master jury said.

“In a time of climate crisis, it offers an excellent solution for autonomy of energy, while smartly reinterpreting the arrangement and materials of a traditional Japanese house.”

House (rural) project of the year: Jiang Deng Lu by Shisuo Design Office

Shisuo Design Office won rural house of the year for Jiang Deng Lu in Anhui, China.

This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result

The compact building is raised partially on stilts to look as though it is floating above its sloped riverside site and made using stainless-steel offcuts salvaged from the client’s own factory.

“This project sits very delicately in its context and is beautiful as a result,” said the judges.

“Innovative in its use of available materials, the project is highly resolved, with incredible quality of light and generosity of space despite a small footprint.”

Housing project of the year: La Querola by Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos

Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos won housing project of the year for La Querola in Ordino, Andorra.

A deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core.

Made up of seven irregularly shaped blocks embedded into the sloping valley and clad in locally sourced slate, the building’s facades feature recessed windows and openings revealing outdoor terraces.

The judges commended the development’s trend-bucking design as a “deliberately expressionist project, celebrating forms that are not repeatable”.

“It’s a deliberate provocation against the salami-type housing where repetition is at the core. It’s unconventional, unique, controversial, and a very strong statement,” they said.

Recently, a fire damaged all seven buildings in the uninhabited development. The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

House renovation of the year: Haniyasu House by Aatismo

Local architecture studio Aatismo won house renovation of the year for Haniyasu House, a home in the coastal town of Kamakura, Japan.

It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability

The project saw the single-storey home, originally built in 1967, stripped back to its timber frame after a typhoon had left it structurally unsound, and boldly characterised with rough walls streaked with clay, soil and metal powders to evoke ceramic glazes.

The judges praised the project’s sensitivity to “the history of both the architecture and its owners”.

“It is aesthetic but also functional, cleverly improving seismic stability,” they added.

House extension of the year: Golmorad by ZAV Architects

Iranian studio ZAV Architects won house extension of the year for its project featuring a series of overlapping arches shifts in colour from terracotta to blue in Tehran, Iran.

It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life.

Transforming the residence from a weekend villa into a permanent home, its arched series of overlapping arched roofs appears as if organically growing from the home.

The judges found the extension to be “playful with a sense of freedom,” adding that, “it doesn’t manipulate the old house in any way, but instead seems to organically extend it in a very unpredictable direction.”

“It’s clever and fun, with colours that reveal an intent to enjoy life,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Civic project of the year: Zando Central Market by Think Tank Architecture

French studio Think Tank Architecture won civic project of the year for its geometric brick-and-concrete market in Kinshasa, Democratic Republic of Congo.

A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves

The new building, with space for 20,000 vendors, replaces a historic market on the same site in the capital that was demolished after insufficient maintenance and an overwhelming number of vendors left it unfit for purpose.

“A bold and strong project with really interesting architectural moves, and a capacity to serve the community in a really large-scale way,” said the master jury.

“It has a variety within it to allow a lot of activity to take place, with materials that are simple but sustainable.”

Cultural project of the year: Ismaili Center Houston by Farshid Moussavi Architecture

Farshid Moussavi Architects won cultural project of the year for its Ismaili Center in Houston, United States.

A very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner

The building and its sprawling gardens is the first Ismaili Center in the US and is one of several around the world commissioned by the current Imam, or spiritual leader, of the Shia Ismaili Muslim community to serve as a place of worship and cultural exchange.

The judges praised it as a “very successful community space that has reinterpreted and reimagined the Ismaili-centric typology in a very contemporary rather than self-referential manner”.

“It has a stunning relationship to light, and incredible detailing and materiality,” they added.

Workplace project (small) of the year: Carpenter’s Home by Primary Architects

Chinese studio Primary Architects won small workplace project of the year for its undulating timber roof-topped studio in Xinyang, China.

The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities

The project, a local carpenter’s studio, was designed by the practice to incorporate the craftsman’s studio, as well as a woodcraft workshop that is also open to the public.

“A beautiful project that goes above and beyond the brief,” commended the judges.

“The architecture speaks of its function, offering space that cleverly facilitates different activities.”

Workplace project (large) of the year: Florentia Village by Turner Works

Architecture studio Turner Works won large workplace project of the year for Florentia Village, London.

Well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour

The practice transformed an old textile manufacturing site in London’s Harringay Warehouse District into a creative hub that offers flexible workshops, studios and industrial units ranging from 46 to 1,400 square metres, alongside community spaces and a cafe.

The judges praised it as “well-thought out in terms of programme, layout and use of materials and colour,” as well as the buildings being “highly flexible, with spaces designed to reinforce a sense of community”.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Education project of the year: Prestige University by Sanjay Puri Architects

Sanjay Puri Architects won education project of the year for its sprawling brick-clad university building in Indore, India.

In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould

Referencing traditional stepped wells found in the country, its defining feature is its 9,000-square-metre walkable roof, which comprises 463 stepped platforms that can be used as individual social spaces or as a singular auditorium for up to 9,000 people

“This project creates its own universe,” said the master jury.

“In a country with a tradition of beautiful campuses, but where most new constructions are based on western typologies, this one breaks the mould,” they continued.

“The massing of the roof reduces scale and creates interesting courtyards, creating spaces that feel appropriate for both the place and its climate.”

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Heritage project of the year: Olympics Utilities by Chartier-Corbasson Architects

French studio Chartier-Corbasson Architectes won heritage project of the year for its transformation of a neglected underground passage beneath Paris, France.

It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant

Located in a passage beneath the Trocadero Gardens, the studio created a public restroom, using an industrial-feeling palette of stainless and weathered steel to highlight its thoughtful, utilitarian design while giving it a new purpose.

“It was a joy to see so much love put into a building typology that we might typically consider unimportant,” said the judges.

“The project creates architectural character, while also preserving a connection to 19th-century futuristic architecture. Unusual, but iconic.”

Hospitality project of the year: Perma by Mold Architects

Perma by Mold Architects in Serifos, Greece won hospitality project of the year, sponsored by Sanderson.

There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint

Comprising five guest houses, the rugged retreat on the island of Serifos was constructed by using material extracted during construction to build much of the retreat itself, rather than removing the hillside and building on top of it.

The judges praised its “striking architecture”, noting it as “very innovative in its programmatic possibilities”.

“There is an economy of means in its relationship to the topography, which cleverly reduces the overall footprint,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Infrastructure and transport project of the year: Naples Underground Central Station by Miralles Tagliabue EMBT

Spanish architecture studio EMBT won infrastructure and transport project of the year for Naples Underground Central Station in Italy.

A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train

Contrasting its modernist surroundings with a wavy timber roof, the 10,000-square-metre building was designed to replace a previously understated metro entrance with a new public plaza that felt more integrated with the surrounding city.

The judges commended the project as a “successful urban space, both elegant and spatially interesting.”

“A rich environment to spend time in, not just catch a train,” they continued. “The use of timber is also impressive.”

Small project of the year: Ring of Bjólfur by Arkibygg Architects

Local studios Arkibygg Architects and Esja Architecture won small project of the year for their mountain viewpoint in Seyðisfjörður, Iceland.

A minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way

Designed to evoke a giant silver ring left on the alleged burial site of a legendary Viking, the viewpoint improves access to a ridge on Mount Bjólfur and celebrates its varied views over the town, valley and surrounding peaks.

The master jury hailed the viewpoint as a “minimal intervention that choreographs the discovery of a landscape in a simple but sophisticated way,” adding that, “the minimal use of material maximises the experience”.

Mixed-use project of the year: York Minster Centre of Excellence by Tonkin Liu

Architecture studio Tonkin Liu won mixed-use project of the year for its two timber buildings on either side of a Grade I-listed Gothic cathedral in York, United Kingdom.

The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space

Named The Centre of Excellence for Heritage Craft Skills, the buildings include the rectangular Heritage Quad and the triangular Technology Hub, both of which give working stonemasons views of the historic York Minster cathedral.

“There is a real honesty in the combination of buildings, with a unique roofing structure,” said the judges.

“The materiality speaks to the programming of the building, inspiring a new generation of makers using the space,” they added.

Landscape and urban design of the year: Parque del Jaguar by Colectivo C733

Mexican studio Colectivo C733 won landscape and urban design of the year for its work across Parque del Jaguar in Tulum, Mexico.

Despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects

The project aims to safeguard one of the region’s important habitats for jaguars, whose movement through the landscape had become disrupted by roads, development and tourism.

It features an 18-kilometre-long limestone wall that allows wildlife to pass through while protecting more than 1,000 hectares of forest, as well as a network of boundaries, access points and visitor facilities intended to protect the animals’ habitat while allowing people to explore the area.

The judges praised the project as “rooted in its context, made for locals as well as tourists,” adding that, “despite limited budget and materials, the interventions create an intimate experience with the landscape, successfully addressing water scarcity, indigenous planting and flexibility for different community projects.”

Sustainable building of the year: Rammed Earth House by Tuckey Design Studio

Rammed Earth house by Tuckey Design Studio in Wiltshire, United Kingdom, won sustainable building of the year, sponsored by Michelmersh.

Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe

Built on the site of a former brickworks, the rural country house was constructed from both the clay underfoot and an aggregate made from crushed demolition waste to form unstabilised rammed earth walls.

As a form of earth construction that is largely untested at such scale in the UK, the judges commended the project as “a radical example of material innovation”.

“Although large for a two-person house, it is an incredible testbed that could pave the way for more rammed earth architecture in Europe,” they said.

The project also won its category for the 2026 public vote.

Sustainable renovation of the year: De Nederlandsche Bank by Mecanoo

Dutch firm Mecanoo won sustainable renovation of the year for its major renovation of the Netherlands’ central bank in Amsterdam.

An admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building

The project involved dismantling a 14-storey tower and opening up the former gold vault, seeing a complete retrofit of De Nederlandsche Bank, a 1968 structure that some had described as the nation’s ugliest building.

The renovation was praised as “an admirable transformation of a brutalist-era building,” by the master jury, who also noted its efforts to adapt it to a different use “while also addressing material and energy concerns.”

#8917. 7 Tips for Building a Healthy Diet With Canned, Frozen, and Packaged Goods

Certain influencers have built entire social media empires out of making everything from scratch. Oftentimes, their videos carry an implicit sense of moral superiority, suggesting that you’re not a good parent (or at least not as good as them) if you’re resorting to pre-packaged store-bought items. Those who pick their own produce and painstakingly hand-craft their own candy necklaces simply work harder, love their children more, are fundamentally better.

But this suggestion is hardly fair. For the vast majority of people—meaning those who don’t make their living off of wellness content or have near-endless amounts of time and money to burn—canned, frozen, and packaged stuff is almost always a far more practical option. “Groceries are a fortune,” after all, Anthea Levi, MS, RD, a Brooklyn-based health writer and the founder of Alive+Well Nutrition, tells SELF—and fresh items tend to be the most expensive, as a trip to the produce section of the supermarket will readily prove.

Besides the lower price point, canned, frozen, and packaged foods have one other major advantage: their staying power. “You can keep them in your freezer for months, so that often gives people confidence” in the purchase, since they know they don’t have an expiration date hanging over their head, Desiree Nielsen, RD, a recipe developer with a focus on plant-based nutrition, tells SELF. This, in turn, leads to reduced food waste: “Fresh salad greens are notorious for going slimy in the fridge, but you’ll never have that issue with frozen spinach. Ditto for fish. Fresh fish needs to be cooked ASAP before it turns, while frozen fish and canned or tinned fish last until you’re ready to use them,” Levi says.

Nielsen also takes issue with the basic idea that these options are somehow inherently inferior—“a big, big misconception,” in her eyes. “There has been a lot of confusion about the nature of these foods in general. Just because something is processed or packaged does not mean it’s unhealthy,” she says.

In other words, canned, frozen, or packaged items are often perfectly fine to include in your diet—and you shouldn’t feel embarrassed, ashamed, or inadequate if they make frequent appearances in your meals (or if they’re your first resort over fresh). “Constant access to fresh foods is, unfortunately, a luxury. If canned, frozen, or packaged items are the only way you’re able to put a fruit or vegetable on your plate, go for it,” Levi says. But if you’re still concerned about the health aspect, there are a few key ways to maximize the nutritional value and improve the overall experience. Here’s what to know to make the most of your freezer stash.

“Typically, the fewer ingredients, the better,” Levi says—a rule of thumb to consider while shopping. While canned, frozen, and packaged items have a reputation for being ultra-processed—rife with additives and lower in nutritional value—there are actually plenty out there “that are made from just one or two whole-food ingredients, such as canned peas, frozen fruit, and canned salmon,” Levi says. “These are as close to fresh foods as you can get, and just as nutritious.” Many jarred peanut butters only contain dry roasted peanuts and salt, for example. (By contrast, Ritz peanut butter crackers, which have an ingredients list several rows long, are a very different story.)

That said, this issue can be nuanced. “Just because an ingredient looks fancy or technical or like a chemical does not necessarily mean that it's bad for you,” Nielsen points out. Many processed foods—including bread, milk, and breakfast cereal—are fortified with healthy vitamins and minerals that you might not otherwise consume enough of in your diet. Take vitamin C—which may appear under the name “ascorbic acid”—as an example. “You might not recognize that what you’re looking at is vitamin C, so you don't want to scare yourself off of potentially nutritious and valuable food because you see things on the ingredients label that you don't recognize,” Nielsen says.

In Nielsen’s experience, canned foods are often considered even less “healthy” than frozen, but the stigma isn’t necessarily warranted. Canned beans, which boast fiber, plant-based protein, and minerals like iron and zinc, are an excellent example of a canned food that amounts to an “incredible nutrition source,” she says. Still, this category does have one major drawback: Staples like veggies, soups, and, yes, beans can contain a significant amount of sodium, a mineral that can cause high blood pressure and related issues like heart disease and stroke when overconsumed. Tinned fish like TikTok’s beloved sardines can suffer from the same issue, as the brine inside the tin can be heavy on added salt as well.

Given that many brands offer sodium-sensitive alternatives, try to prioritize those options instead to keep your sodium intake in check and avoid potential health consequences, according to Nielsen. Look for labels like “No salt added,” “Low sodium,” or even “No sodium” to steer you in the right direction. If you can’t find anything fitting that bill at your local store, draining and rinsing canned products before use can also drastically cut down on the sodium content—by up to 40%, according to some estimates. (Just keep in mind this method may also cause losses in other nutrients, like vitamin C.)

“In terms of packaged and processed foods, I'm always looking for a couple of nutrients to minimize and a couple of nutrients to optimize,” Nielsen says. Sodium is one to limit or avoid, as we’ve already covered, but there are others too—like added sugars and saturated fat. “Peaches that come canned in sugary syrup aren’t as nutritious as peaches that come canned in water, or are purchased frozen or fresh,” for example, Levi says.

On the other hand, when you’re reading over a nutrition facts label, “what you want to see is fiber,” Nielsen says—and “protein is a big bonus.” Multiple vitamins and minerals in a product is also often a positive sign. Even breakfast cereals, which are often thought of as unhealthy, “can be incredible sources of minerals like iron and zinc—things that we need that help to keep our metabolism running, that keep us energized,” Nielsen says.

Trying to decide between two (or more) similar products? Comparing and contrasting the ingredients can help you narrow it down, according to Nielsen. Take breakfast cereal: You’ll want to ask yourself, “‘Which one of these cereals gives me the most fiber, the most protein, has the least sugar?’” she says. In this case, the relative content of vitamins and minerals can also be a helpful clue. Seeing that a cereal contains 10% to 20% of your recommended dietary allowance, as many do, can be “your sort of gut check that this is actually a really nutritious food,” Nielsen says.

Even though frozen veggies are affordable and durable, they do have one big downside compared to fresh: Their taste and texture can take a hit—and, in turn, “you do have to adjust your cooking somewhat,” Nielsen says. To prevent sogginess, cook frozen veggies from frozen rather than letting them defrost first, according to Levi. And you’ll want to use heat-based cooking methods (like air-frying, baking, roasting, and stir-frying) “as opposed to water-based methods like boiling or steaming,” she says.

“Many of us are working more than ever before—maybe working two or three jobs—and we don't have a lot of time to put a home-cooked meal on the table,” Nielsen says. Strategically pairing your canned, frozen, and packaged items is an easy way to boost efficiency in the kitchen without sacrificing nutritional value. If you’re having canned soup for dinner, you can dump in a can of lentils to boost the fiber and protein, for example. (Bonus tip: You can also use this approach to stretch out your leftovers. Need a batch of spaghetti to last longer? Toss some frozen peas on top or some frozen broccoli on the side.)

“Stocking your freezer and pantry with budget-friendly canned, frozen, and packaged items can help make balanced meals a breeze,” Levi says. Follow the tried-and-true “plate method” to guarantee a nutritious result, according to Nielsen: Reserve a quarter of your plate for whole grains or starchy vegetables, another quarter for protein, and the remaining half for fruits and non-starchy veggies. You could make rolled oats with chia seeds, frozen berries, and peanut butter for breakfast, or pasta with tinned sardines and frozen broccoli for dinner, for example, Levi says. “It sounds way too simple, but it is backed by so much science to help you balance your diet without counting anything,” Nielsen says. “As long as you stick to that plate method, you will be eating a nourishing diet”—yes, even if your ingredients don’t come to you direct.

#8916. How to Use Jojoba Oil for Hair: Expert Tips for Stunning Results

Jojoba oil is a must-have for moisturizing shampoos and skincare products.

The slippery oil is squeezed out of jojoba plant seeds. These plants are shrubs that pop up around the desert-y spots ofArizona, southern California, and Mexico.

Though it’s been used as a natural remedy for centuries, jojoba oil is having a major hair moment right now.

Keep reading to learn how to use it for strong, shiny hair and a healthy scalp.

“Jojoba oil is incredibly nourishing,” says Mayara Macedo, a hairstylist and scalp specialist in NYC. “It’s a natural oil that closely resembles the sebum our skin and scalp produce,” Macedo explains.

Because of this, Macedo says it’s super compatible with our bodies and works great as a balancing treatment — whether you have an oily or dry scalp.

While its proven benefits mainly revolve around its help with scalp health, jojoba oil can also strengthen and moisturize hair. However, it’s not the go-to pick for improving hair loss (that’s usually minoxidil).

If you’re dealing with dryness, jojoba oil is fantastic for adding moisture to your scalp,” Macedo says.

“Its natural hydrating properties help restore balance, leaving everything healthier and more manageable.”

“Jojoba oil has been known for its antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties in addition to its conditioning and emollient properties,” says Kseniya Kobets, MD, board-certified dermatologist and Director of Cosmetics Dermatology at Montefiore Einstein Advanced Care.

These properties help out with dry, irritating dandruff.

This also explains jojoba oil‘s Mexican Indian history as a treatment for sores, which eventually caused researchers to flag its potential for improving skin conditions like acne and psoriasis (but please see a dermatologist for proven treatment options).

Though many say that jojoba oil grows hair, this claim is probably tossed around because it helps moisturize hair follicles — which can keep dryness at bay.

A dry environment can be a breeding ground for breakage, hair loss, and dandruff.

Also, your split ends say hello — jojoba oil can help by restoring hair health overall.

“If your scalp gets oily quickly after washing,” Macedo says, “It could be because your scalp is overcompensating, thinking it doesn’t have enough moisture and needs to produce more oil.”

She says adding jojoba oil helps signal to your scalp that it has enough, which can slow down excess oil production.

Although you can apply jojoba oil to the length and tips of your hair, Macedo says she prefers to use it only for the scalp, saying that other oils, like argan oil, will work better for the length.

Here;s how Macedo recommends using jojoba oil:

You can also buy shampoos or conditions that already have it!

Macedo says you can apply jojoba oil to wet or dry hair, depending on your goal.

“If you want to lock in moisture and add shine, you can try applying it to damp hair.” However, she doesn’t recommend this because it’s easy to accidentally apply too much or distribute it unevenly on wet hair, which she says can leave your hair feeling heavy and greasy.

“Applying it to dry hair reduces frizz and adds a light shine to styled hair,” she suggests.

Kobets recommends using oils overnight for extended exposure. However, she points out this can get messy (RIP pillowcases), so you can always apply them for a few hours and wash them off before bed.

Macedo also suggests being mindful of the amount you use — too much can make your hair look greasy, especially true for fine hair. “For a lightweight finish, start with a small amount and focus on the ends of your hair. But again, I’d recommend jojoba oil for the scalp and argan oil for the hair,” Macedo adds.

“If you’re using jojoba oil as a pre-wash treatment to balance scalp oil or as a deep conditioner, apply it before washing,” Macedo explains. “If you’re using it as a leave-in conditioner or frizz-tamer, you can apply it to freshly washed hair — careful not to apply too much.”

Kobets suggests washing the scalp after using oils, noting that her patients don’t always prefer to use them because they can reduce hair volume for some.

Kobets says that someone with a dehydrated scalp and coarse hair may want to leave the oil in to hydrate the scalp better. “People with fine or oily scalps usually want to wash the oils out,” she adds.

Jojoba oil is a natural moisturizing ingredient known for improving scalp health. It can also add shine and help strengthen your locks.

It’s not the move for improving hair loss, however.

Do a patch test to make sure you aren’t allergic first! Then you’re good to glow.

#8915. Discover this year's Dezeen Awards Designers of the Year

Dezeen has announced the six winners of Dezeen Awards 2026 Designers of the Year at this evening’s ceremony in London, which include Lina Ghotmeh, Keiji Ashizawa and Yinka Ilori.

Our Designers of the Year awards recognise the best emerging and established talent whose innovative work has made a notable impact on the industry across architecture, interiors and design.

This year, Ghotmeh took home the architect of the year award, while studio duo Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo were named emerging architect of the year.

Interior designer of the year was awarded to Tokyo-based Ashizawa, and Australian designer Yasmine Ghoniem was named emerging interior designer of the year.

London-based Ilori won designer of the year with Stockholm-based Simon Skinner named emerging designer of the year.

Read more about the Designers of the Year below:

Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet.

Ghotmeh, who is the founder of architecture practice Lina Ghotmeh Architecture, is one of the world’s most sought-after architects. Among her high-profile projects was the 2023 Serpentine Pavilion and she was recently appointed to renovate the British Museum’s Western Range galleries.

“From Beirut to Paris and beyond, Lina Ghotmeh creates architecture that feels both rooted in history and entirely of the future,” said the judges.

“Her poetic approach to materials, memory and landscape brings buildings to life with a rare sensitivity to people, place and planet. We anticipate her studio continuing to go from strength to strength.”

Ghotmeh is known for her sustainable and historically rooted designs, including the Stone Garden apartment block in Beruit, which was named architecture project of the year at Dezeen Awards 2021. She has received multiple accolades, including being named on the Time100 Next list in 2025 and winning the 2023 Great Arab Minds Award.

Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.

Emerging architect of the year: Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo

Founded by Japanese architect Shohei Kuma and French‑Spanish architect and urban designer Elsa Escobedo, Kuma&Elsa is an emerging architecture studio with offices in France, Spain and Japan.

“Shohei Kuma and Elsa Escobedo’s emerging practice brings a fresh sense of curiosity to architecture, balancing bold forms and material experimentation with tactility and unexpected gestures,” said the judges.

“Working between Japan and Europe, Kuma and Elsa are creating an architectural vocabulary that feels both regionally distinctive and deeply connected to its surroundings.”

Among the studio’s varied and intriguing work is Nakano House in Japan’s Fukuoka prefecture – an apartment block informed by the design of a traditional Japanese engawa.

His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.

Interior designer of the year: Keiji Ashizawa

Interior designer Ashizawa runs his interdisciplinary, craft-oriented studio based on the ideal of “honest design”. Along with interior spaces, his Tokyo-based studio designs everything from lighting to furniture and products.

“Prolific designer Keiji Ashizawa brings a quiet confidence to interior design, where natural materials, considered details, refined craftsmanship and a sense of calm take centre stage,” said the judges.

“His distinct spaces reveal the beauty in restraint, proving that the most powerful interiors are often those that will quietly stand the test of time.”

Recent work from the studio includes a tea shop in central Shanghai, a holiday home clad in charred cedar in central Japan and a showroom for Japanese furniture brand Karimoku.

Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.

Emerging interior designer of the year: Yasmine Ghoniem

Australian designer Ghoniem has found great success since founding her interior studio YSG in 2020 with the aim of creating bold, holistic design experiences.

“Yasmine Ghoniem takes a bold, instinctive approach to interior design, bringing together rich textures, unexpected colour and cultural references,” said the judges.

“Often challenging convention, her interiors are expressive and distinctive, and full of character, warmth and individuality that defy easy categorisation.”

Among her recent – and varied – designs are a wellness hotel in Bali, the revamp of a Sydney apartment, a warehouse conversion in Sydney designed to evoke the Mojave desert and a bar for gin brand Four Pillars.

Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.

Ilori designs pavilions, installations, pop-ups, products and furniture, all united by a bold use of colour informed by his Nigerian heritage.

“Yinka Ilori injects design with an irresistible dose of colour, humour and optimism, turning everyday objects and spaces into lively celebrations of culture and community,” said the judges.

“Rooted in his British-Nigerian heritage, his exuberant work reminds us that design can be as joyful as it is meaningful, bringing people together through shared experiences and bold creative expression.”

Ilori has designed numerous pavilions, including the Colour Palace in London and an events space for the Estrel Berlin hotel in Germany. On a smaller scale, he has designed products including a watch for Swiss brand MB&F and his own range of branded homeware.

He also recently created an extensive collection of furniture, fabrics and homeware for Dunelm.

Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language.

Emerging designer of the year: Simon Skinner

Swedish designer Skinner is well-known for his furniture, sculpture and installations that explore how materials can be rethought or reused.

“Simon Skinner is a burgeoning talent who brings a fresh perspective to contemporary Scandinavian design, pairing a thoughtful approach to materials with a refined, understated visual language. His work subverts the familiar, creating distinct new objects that hint at an exciting new direction for design.”

Recent examples of his varied, multidisciplinary work include a range of sculptural lights made from second-hand bowls, ashtrays and cat figurines.

Dezeen Awards 2026 in partnership with TrimbleDezeen Awards is the ultimate accolade for architects and designers worldwide. The ninth edition of the annual awards is in partnership with global technology company Trimble. Through connected hardware and software solutions, Trimble helps designers to transform the way they shape spaces and buildings as well as drive productivity in the process. Trimble’s collaboration with Dezeen Awards demonstrates its ongoing commitment to inspiring and supporting creative excellence across the globe.

#8914. The Nordic Pavilion Explores Traditional Craft Through "Painted Matter" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale

The National Museum of Norway has announced Painted Matter as the title of Norway's contribution to the 20th International Architecture Exhibition of the Venice Biennale, scheduled to take place from May 8 to November 21, 2027. Developed by Oslo-based practice Kastler Skjeseth Architects, the exhibition will be presented at the Nordic Pavilion and will explore the role of traditional decorative painting techniques in contemporary architecture, with a focus on material use, architectural expression, and sustainability. The Nordic Pavilion, designed by Norwegian architect Sverre Fehn, is jointly owned by Norway, Sweden, and Finland. For the 2027 edition, the National Museum of Norway is responsible for organizing the Nordic contribution on behalf of Moderna Museet in Stockholm and the Architecture and Design Museum in Helsinki.

Developed by Oslo-based practice Kastler Skjeseth Architects, the exhibition will be presented at the Nordic Pavilion and will explore the role of traditional decorative painting techniques in contemporary architecture, with a focus on material use, architectural expression, and sustainability. For the 2027 edition, the National Museum of Norway is responsible for organizing the Nordic contribution on behalf of Moderna Museet in Stockholm and the Architecture and Design Museum in Helsinki.

The exhibition takes decorative painting as its starting point, looking at techniques such as graining, marbling, and wood staining. Historically, these methods were used to imitate materials that were not readily available locally, allowing craftspeople to give wood and other common surfaces the appearance of more expensive materials. In Norway, for instance, wooden interiors could be painted to resemble marble, reflecting the exchange of craft techniques and aesthetic influences across different regions.

In Norway, for instance, wooden interiors could be painted to resemble marble, reflecting the exchange of craft techniques and aesthetic influences across different regions.

Through these practices, Painted Matter will examine the relationship between traditional craftsmanship and contemporary approaches to construction. The exhibition connects the reuse of existing materials and the consideration of material life cycles with renewed interest in ornament, historical references, and architectural expression. It also considers how decorative painting can transform existing surfaces without requiring the introduction of new materials, bringing traditional techniques into discussions around material scarcity and environmental awareness. The project will further investigate questions of authenticity and material value. Although decorative painting creates surfaces that imitate other materials, the techniques themselves require specialized knowledge and craftsmanship. The exhibition will explore how these distinctions inform perceptions of authenticity and status in architecture, including how the value assigned to materials changes over time.

As part of the exhibition, Italian photographer Stefano Graziani will document decorative painting in traditional Norwegian buildings, covering historical examples, contemporary interpretations, and preserved fragments of this craft tradition. The project will also involve five second-year students from Hjerleid Craft School in Dovre, Norway, which offers training in traditional decorative painting. Drawing on Norwegian and Italian craft traditions, the students will develop architectural surfaces using these techniques as part of their coursework and participate in the installation's realization in Venice.

#8913. 6 Signs Your Skin Needs Medical Attention, Stat

Your skin is your most visible organ, so it’s easy to notice when something seems off. It’s normal to experience some skin issues from time to time, like itchiness, breakouts, or ingrown hairs. But when these skin symptoms stick around, it could be a sign that something more serious is going on.

Many of these skin issues get better with the right at-home remedies or changes in your skin care routine. For example, if dryness pops up when Old Man Winter comes along, slathering on a more intense moisturizer may help.

But if skin symptoms don’t go away with a little self-care — or they return frequently — a chronic skin condition might be the culprit. However, just because you have a lasting symptom or two doesn’t necessarily mean you have a chronic health issue.

Here are the symptoms you should watch for and what they might mean. And if they don’t improve, consider checking in with a dermatologist for a proper diagnosis and a plan of action.

If you wish you had cat claws to satisfy your skin itch, you could be dealing with eczema. Eczema is an umbrella term for several conditions that impact the skin, with atopic dermatitis being the most common.

With most forms of eczema, your skin may show signs of inflammation, such as:

These symptoms may flare up occasionally and then go into periods of remission, where your skin isn’t as irritated.

Allergies can also lead to itchiness. For example, if you’re allergic to a skin care ingredient, a fabric type, a pet, or another allergen, your skin might react as a way to tell you to avoid this trigger.

Ongoing or regular periods of itchiness are a reason to see a dermatologist.

A rash can affect the skin in various ways, including:

A one-off or temporary rash might result from friction or chafing from a new outfit item. It could also be a heat rash when sweat gets trapped in skinfolds or bodily creases.

A persistent rash could be a sign of eczema or allergies. However, different types of rashes can be a sign of other things. For example, a butterfly-shaped (malar) rash across the face is a common sign of an autoimmune disease known as lupus.

If you frequently experience skin rashes, talk with a dermatologist to help you get to the bottom of the issue.

Dry skin can be just that — dry skin. Common causes include:

But if your skin is so dry it makes you want to bathe in a vat of thick moisturizer, it could be a sign of psoriasis.

Psoriasis is an inflammatory skin condition potentially caused by an overactive immune system. It can lead to dry, cracked, or scaling skin. In fact, psoriasis often involves a buildup of scales or plaques on areas like the elbows or knees — though they can occur anywhere.

Psoriasis and eczema are different conditions, but they have overlapping symptoms that mimic each other. So if you experience these symptoms, it’s important to see a dermatologist to identify and treat the underlying cause.

Changes in skin color — including red, brown, gray, or purple patches of skin — can be a sign of various skin issues, including eczema, psoriasis, or allergies. But it can also be a sign of rosacea.

Rosacea typically involves persistent redness that looks like a sunburn or blushing. It may also lead to skin thickening.

The good news? Rosacea is highly treatable. So working with a dermatologist can help you address it.

No one is immune from developing the occasional pimple or ingrown hair. But sometimes, skin bumps can be a sign that something else is going on.

Acne is one of the most common skin conditions that could bring skin bumps like pimples.

Hidradenitis suppurativa (HS) is another condition that causes painful, boil-like lumps to form underneath the skin. These bumps can turn into pus-filled pockets that may connect via tunnels. HS typically shows up in areas of high friction or where skin meets skin, such as the armpits or groin.

Other types of skin bumps may include ingrown hairs, which can get infected and turn into folliculitis.

Talk with a dermatologist to help you address any bothersome skin bumps you may experience.

Common moles are growths that develop when pigment cells (melanocytes) grow in clusters. The average adult has between 10 to 40 common moles.

An irregular mole, also known as a dysplastic nevus, is a type of mole that looks different from your common moles. If you have a dysplastic nevus (or several), schedule regular skin checks with a dermatologist to look for anything suspicious. Be sure to mention any changes in:

These types of changes could be a sign of a form of skin cancer such as melanoma, which occurs in melanocytes. Melanoma can develop anywhere, including on normal-looking skin, a common mole, or a dysplastic nevus.

Skin symptoms — like rashes, bumps, discoloration, dryness, or itchiness — may come and go. But if symptoms stick around or return frequently, consider seeing a dermatologist for an evaluation. Your skin may be telling you that there’s an underlying issue that needs to be addressed.

A dermatologist can provide a proper diagnosis and treatment plan to help reduce, or, in some cases, resolve your skin symptoms. If you don’t currently have a dermatologist, your primary care physician or nurse practitioner can refer you to one.

Last medically reviewed on February 12, 2025

#8912. Isern Serra designs bold colour-blocked interiors for Barcelona pilates studio

Spanish design practice Isern Serra combined organic architectural forms with a vibrant colour palette for Circl, a fitness studio and matcha cafe located in Barcelona’s historic Eixample district.

Set just below street level, the 180-square-metre space was designed to offer an escape from the busy city centre and contains an entrance cafe, reception area, changing rooms, bathrooms and a pilates studio.

“The project began with the idea of bringing together two worlds: pilates and matcha,” Isern Serra told Dezeen.

“Although different in nature, both share a common philosophy centred on wellbeing, balance and the connection between body and mind,” he continued.

“Architecture plays an essential role in this experience, accompanying visitors on a gradual transition from the energy of the city towards a more intimate and introspective environment.”

His studio introduced a series of colour-blocked spaces to guide customers through different phases of the interior, with colours that were specifically chosen to correspond to the function and tone of each area.

“This vision of wellbeing takes shape through a carefully choreographed sequence of spaces, where each change in level, colour and atmosphere guides users away from the bustle of the city and towards an increasingly introspective environment,” said Serra.

Serra combined cream banquette seating with dark wooden tables and alabaster sconces to create a calm, meditative environment for the cafe part of the space. A sculptural, mirrored service counter was also incorporated to reflect natural light around the space.

To signal the transition into the pilates studio, the designers introduced a deep-green reception hallway with tiered seating blocks and a spherical light installation.

The bright green circulation area is connected by an open archway and features curved architectural volumes that house the changing rooms, bathrooms and a water fountain.

Another rounded archway then leads to the main studio.

The main pilates studio was designed as a white space to reflect the coloured light from a sculptural LED light installation attached to the vaulted ceiling.

The aim was to create diverse exercise environments and enable the lighting to control the mood and energy of the space.

“The white surfaces act as a neutral canvas for coloured light, allowing different hues to transform the atmosphere,” Serra said.

“This system also offers flexibility for brand collaborations, as the lighting can be adapted to reflect different identities and experiences,” he added.

In the studio, the designers used mirrored walls to create the illusion of a circular room and added full-length perimeter curtains to soften the space’s texture.

Other interior projects recently featured on Dezeen include Matteo Thun designs for Milan’s Torre Velasca skyscraper and SABO’s design of an apartment on Manhattan’s Lower East Side.

#8910. How Taking a GLP-1 Could Affect Your Bone Health

When it comes to treating obesity, type 2 diabetes, and other chronic health conditions, GLP-1 agonist drugs—such as Ozempic, Zepbound, and Wegovy—have been a game changer for literally millions of Americans.

But as with any medication, these drugs can deliver unwelcome side effects. And a recent study that just garnered a bunch of attention raised the possibility of new ones.

The research, which was presented at the 2026 American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons annual meeting in March and has not yet been peer-reviewed, found a link between GLP-1 use and increased risk of bone issues, including osteoporosis (weak, brittle bones) and osteomalacia (soft bones). The study also found a link between GLP-1 use and heightened risk of gout, a type of arthritis that causes pain and swelling in the joints.

The lead study author said he became interested in whether GLP-1s might affect bone and other connective tissue after some of his patients “developed serious tendon tears following relatively minor injuries,” according to NBC News. After analyzing five years of medical records from nearly 147,000 adults with type 2 diabetes and obesity, the study authors concluded that GLP-1 use was associated with a “significantly increased” risk of osteoporosis, osteomalacia, and gout.

Of course, this news is likely unsettling for anyone on these medications. But should we be legit worried about these findings? And how exactly could GLP-1s harm bone health in the first place? We tapped two experts for answers, along with practical tips for protecting bone health while taking GLP-1s.

First, some relieving news: As of now, there is “no sound scientific evidence” that suggests GLP-1s directly increase the risk of osteoporosis or osteomalacia, Marci Laudenslager, MD, an obesity medicine physician with The Johns Hopkins Healthful Eating, Activity & Weight Program, tells SELF. (Same goes for gout, she adds.)

Dr. Laudenslager, who was not involved in the study, points out that it was observational in nature, meaning it looked at correlation…not causation. “While well-conducted observational studies can reveal a potential relationship between a medication and a clinical outcome, they cannot determine whether a medication directly causes that clinical outcome,” she explains.

Another limitation of the study is that it relied on medical records alone, which means it assumed that all patients who were prescribed GLP-1s, as noted in their medical records, were actually taking the drug. In reality, many patients who are prescribed GLP-1s are unable to take them because of cost or medication shortages, Dr. Laudenslager says. Moreover, people who do start taking don’t always continue due to insurance, cost, or problems tolerating the drug, she adds.

Beyond that, the study didn’t take into account factors that commonly impact bone health, like exercise habits, nutritional habits, and other lifestyle factors, Kelyssa Hall, an exercise physiologist and certified strength and conditioning specialist at Hospital for Special Surgery, tells SELF. “These factors can play a huge role in bone health with or without the addition of GLP-1s.” The study also didn’t account for certain endocrine conditions, cancers, alcohol use, family history, and steroid use–all of which can also play a role in bone health, Dr. Laudenslager adds. And the study didn’t note which specific GLP-1 drug people used and the dosage, she adds.

Lastly, the study findings have not yet been peer reviewed–a step that Dr. Laudenslager describes it as “essential” in the scientific process. As Hall puts it: The study “highlights the need for more research on these topics.”

Okay, so that particular study has its limitations. But other research supports the notion that these drugs may be linked with declining bone health. So…is there actual cause for concern?

According to Dr. Laudenslager and Hall, taking GLP1-s can indeed decrease bone density for some people. But that’s likely due to the volume and rate at which people lose weight while on these drugs—and not anything specific to the medication itself, Dr. Laudenslager says.

“When you take GLP-1s, there can be rapid weight loss which means there is less load being carried around on the skeleton,” Hall says. “Bone formation or strengthening is improved with load to the skeletal system,” she explains, “so losing weight decreases the regular load on the bones overall.”

Over time, this decrease in loading can translate to a decrease in bone density, Dr. Laudenslager says. But, again, this isn’t unique to GLP-1s: “Significant weight loss through any mechanism—lifestyle change, medications, or surgery—can impact metabolism as a whole and bone metabolism, in particular,” she says. Basically, whenever you lose a bunch of weight—regardless of how you lost those pounds—there’s always a risk of bone loss.

In short, while it’s true that some people taking GLP-1s have had changes to their bone health, these changes seem to “be driven primarily by magnitude of weight loss rather than a direct, negative consequence of the medications themselves,” Dr. Laudenslager says. That said, the use of GLP-1s and bone health “is an active area of study,” she adds. More research is needed to fully understand the impact of GLP-1s on bone density.

Resistance training is important for pretty much everyone—and that includes folks on GLP-1s. One of its many benefits is that it’s been shown to improve bone density, Hall says. That means it can be a helpful strategy to bolster bone health when you’re on a GLP-1. Plus, strength training can help guard against muscle loss that can happen when you’re losing weight. “Retaining muscle mass is important for strength and stability,” she says. And it can also help support your overall metabolism, she adds, which can help your body sustain weight loss results for the long haul.

If you’re new to strength training, Dr. Laudenslager recommends gradually building up to a routine of two to three sessions a week, with at least a day off in between each workout to allow your muscles the time they need to recover. Before getting started though, make sure to check with your doctor or other medical provider so they can advise what type of workouts are safe and recommended for you.

A common side effect of GLP-1s is appetite suppression, which can sometimes lead people to follow a really low calorie diet. Calorie restriction can suppress bone growth and increase the risk of fractures, according to research, which is one of the reasons you want to make sure you’re still eating enough to support your overall health while on a GLP-1. “Hunger is an essential hormonal cue we all need in order to sustain health,” Dr. Laudenslager says. The ideal amount of calories is highly individualized, but if you’re unsure that you’re getting what you need, bring it up with your doctor or another qualified expert, such as a registered dietitian.

Protein is often touted for its muscle-building benefits, but it’s also vital for bone health, as it helps to build bone mass. The recommended dietary allowance for adults is 0.8 grams of protein per kilograms of bodyweight a day—a general guideline that Dr. Laudenslager also suggests for people taking GLP-1s. She suggests a slightly higher intake for people at greater risk of bone health issues (such as older adults and postmenopausal women) and lesser amounts in people with kidney disease. Just make sure that as you prioritize protein, you don’t skimp on important components of a well-rounded diet, including fiber, water, healthy fats, and essential vitamins, minerals, and nutrients, she adds.

Rapid weight loss can be harmful for bone health, so to mitigate this risk, strive for a more gradual reduction in pounds. The recommended rate of weight loss depends on your starting weight, but as a general guideline, Dr. Laudenslager recommends losing 5% to 10% of your total weight over the course of about six months. This translates to an average of about 0.5 to 2 pounds lost a week. So if you notice that taking a GLP-1 is causing you to lose weight at a faster pace, bring it up with your doctor. They may want to adjust your medication dosing to help slow your weight loss rate into a more ideal, gradual range.

Bone loss isn’t an overnight thing. In fact, clinically significant bone loss typically happens over the course of years, Dr. Laudenslager says. “This means there are a wealth of opportunities throughout a person’s weight loss journey to prevent and treat bone loss early on if it’s detected through surveillance.” So if you have any bone health concerns, mention them to your doctor (though hopefully your provider is proactively thinking about this too).

On that note, Dr. Laudenslager strongly encourages people interested in obesity treatment to seek care from a board-certified obesity medicine physician. She recommends the American Board of Obesity Medicine and the Obesity Action Coalition websites as resources for finding a board-certified provider.

GLP-1s can be a true game-changer for people struggling with chronic health conditions. Unfortunately, there’s still a lot of societal stigma and misunderstanding surrounding obesity, including the misconception that “anti-obesity medications are dangerous and should be avoided,” Dr. Laudenslager says. In truth, though? “The medication side effects are quite manageable when prescribed by providers who are well-versed in current practice guidelines,” she says.

Picture this: you're standing at the gate for your Boston weekend trip, and the person next to you just swiped their credit card for $280 to book the exact same seat you're sitting in — a seat that cost you 7,500 Avios and maybe $5.60 in taxes. That's the British Airways Avios short-haul sweet spot in action, and once you see it, you can never unsee it. This is the redemption the ChooseFI community quietly uses to stretch their points further than almost any other domestic award. While everyone else is chasing first-class international awards (which are spectacular, don't get us wrong), this sweet spot lets you turn a modest points balance into a steady stream of nearly free regional flights — year-round, on American Airlines metal, with zero fuel surcharges. Here's the math that makes it click: A last-minute nonstop flight from New York (JFK/LGA) to Boston Logan or Los Angeles (LAX) to San Francisco typically runs anywhere from $150 to $300 in cash. You're paying that for roughly a one-hour flight — the kind of trip where by the time the flight attendant hands you a drink, you're already starting your descent. British Airways prices that same flight at a flat **7,500 Avios**. At a $200 cash fare, that's **2.67 cents per point (CPP)** — well above the standard valuation most programs offer for domestic economy. At a $300 last-minute fare, you're looking at **4 cents per point**, which is exceptional for any award program, let alone a simple domestic booking. The pricing inefficiency is hiding in plain sight: British Airways uses a **distance-based award chart**, which means short flights cost proportionally fewer points. The U.S. domestic short-haul zone (under 650 miles) sits at 7,500 Avios one-way — a price that hasn't ballooned with inflation the way cash fares have. Every time airfare spikes for a holiday weekend or a last-minute booking, your Avios redemption looks better and better. For the FI-minded traveler, this redemption is pure arbitrage: you're converting transferable points that cost you perhaps 1–1.5 cents each to earn into travel worth 2–4 cents each in real-world value. That's a 2–4x return, consistently, on routes you'd likely be flying anyway.

The magic here lives inside British Airways' distance-based award chart — and understanding why it's structured this way is the 'aha moment' that turns a confusing loyalty program into a tool you actually want to use.

Most U.S. airline programs (Delta, United, American) have largely abandoned distance-based pricing in favor of dynamic or zone-based awards that tend to price popular routes higher. British Airways never fully made that switch for partner awards. Their Avios chart still prices flights primarily by the number of miles flown between origin and destination. A flight under 650 miles costs 7,500 Avios one-way in economy — full stop. It doesn't matter if it's a Tuesday in February or the Sunday after Thanksgiving. The chart price holds.

The Partner Piece: Why You're Booking AA, Not BA

Here's the critical nuance that trips up new users: British Airways charges notoriously high fuel surcharges on its own operated flights. We're talking $300–800+ in carrier-imposed fees on top of the Avios. That would completely wipe out the value of this redemption. But when you book American Airlines-operated flights through British Airways Avios, those surcharges disappear entirely. AA does not pass fuel surcharges to partner award bookings. Your out-of-pocket cost is typically just the government taxes — often $5–15 each way.

This is the non-negotiable rule: always book AA metal through British Airways Avios, not BA-operated flights.

Avios are one of the most accessible award currencies in the ecosystem. You can transfer from four major transferable points programs at a 1:1 ratio:

Marriott Bonvoy also transfers to Avios at a 3:1 ratio (3 Marriott points = 1 Avios), and Marriott throws in a 5,000 Avios bonus for every 60,000 Marriott points transferred. That's a less efficient path for this redemption, but worth knowing.

The 355-day booking window means you can transfer and book nearly a full year in advance — critical for holiday travel or high-demand routes.

British Airways allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. That means you could theoretically fly into one city and out of a nearby city without paying for two separate awards — useful if you're exploring a region and want flexibility. For short domestic hops, this opens up creative itinerary options that pure point-to-point programs don't allow.

Before you touch your Avios balance, go to aa.com and run a standard flight search for your route. When the results load, look specifically for flights labeled 'Web Special' or filter by lowest MileSAAver awards. You're searching for American's own award inventory — the same inventory British Airways can see and book. If AA shows saver-level availability (the lowest award tier), British Airways will almost certainly be able to book it too.

This step saves you frustration. Don't transfer points until you've confirmed the flight you want is bookable at the saver level.

Double-check that your route qualifies for the 7,500 Avios tier by confirming it's under 650 miles. NYC to Boston is about 187 miles. LAX to SFO is about 337 miles. Both qualify easily. A quick Google search — '[City A] to [City B] flight distance miles' — gives you the straight-line distance. When in doubt, routes you'd describe as 'short regional hops' within the same metro corridor will almost always qualify.

Go to britishairways.com, log into (or create) your Executive Club account, and run an Avios award search for the same route and dates. You should see the American Airlines flight(s) appear at 7,500 Avios + a small tax amount — typically $5–$15. If the flight shows up here, you're ready to book.

Once you've confirmed availability, it's time to transfer. Here's what to do based on your points currency:

Important: Only transfer what you need. Points transferred to British Airways cannot be moved back.

Return to BA's award search (refresh if needed), select your American Airlines flight, and complete the booking. You'll pay the Avios from your balance plus the small tax amount with a credit card. You'll receive an American Airlines confirmation number, which you can use at aa.com to manage your reservation, select seats, and add TSA PreCheck or Known Traveler Numbers.

Let's make this concrete. It's mid-October and you want to visit a college friend in Boston for the weekend — flying out of New York's JFK on a Friday evening, returning Sunday afternoon.

You pull up Google Flights. Friday evening nonstops from JFK to BOS? The cheapest is $189. The convenient 6:30 PM departure on American Airlines is $229. Sunday afternoon return is another $199. Round-trip cash cost: $428.

You check aa.com and confirm both flights show saver-level award availability. You open British Airways' site and find:

You transfer 15,000 Chase Ultimate Rewards points to British Airways — it arrives instantly. You book both flights through BA, receive your AA confirmation numbers, and log into aa.com to select your seats.

If those flights had crept up to $300 each (not unusual around Columbus Day weekend), you'd be looking at 4 cents per point — outstanding for a domestic economy booking.

You're on a standard American Airlines narrow-body — likely a Boeing 737 or Airbus A319. It's economy, which for a 45-minute flight is entirely appropriate. You'll get a beverage service, overhead bin space, and you land at the same gate, use the same terminal, and have the same on-time performance as any other passenger on that plane. The difference is that they paid $229 and you paid $5.60 plus some points that cost you roughly $150 to earn through everyday spending.

That's the FI mindset applied to travel: same experience, radically different cost.

Do This: Book Up to 355 Days Out for Holiday Travel BA's booking window opens 355 days in advance, and American releases its best saver space early. If you're targeting Thanksgiving weekend, Christmas, or a peak summer Friday, set a calendar reminder to search at the 355-day mark. Award seats on popular routes at peak times go fast.

Do This: Use the Open-Jaw Rule Creatively BA allows open-jaw routing on Avios awards. If you're flying into NYC but want to return from a different airport — say JFK inbound and EWR outbound — you may be able to structure this as a single open-jaw award rather than two separate bookings. Worth exploring for multi-city weekend trips.

Avoid This: Booking BA-Operated Flights with This Strategy This cannot be overstated — BA's own flights carry $300–800+ in carrier-imposed surcharges. If you accidentally book a British Airways codeshare or BA-metal flight instead of an American Airlines-operated flight, you'll owe hundreds in fees. Always verify the operating carrier before confirming. Look for 'Operated by American Airlines' in the booking details.

Avoid This: Transferring Points Before Confirming Availability Points transferred to British Airways are one-way and permanent. Never transfer until you have eyes on the specific flight, date, and saver availability you want. The 30-second search on BA's site before transferring is non-negotiable.

Do This: Keep Your Account Active Avios expire after 36 months of account inactivity. If you accumulate Avios for a future trip, make sure to earn or redeem at least a small amount every three years. Even a small shopping portal purchase through the BA Executive Club keeps your balance alive.

Do This: Stack with Other Short Hops Think about recurring trips in your life — quarterly visits to family, annual conferences, weekend trips to a nearby city. This sweet spot isn't just for one redemption; it's a repeatable system. A modest Avios balance of 30,000–45,000 points could cover three to six regional roundtrips per year.

Most U.S. airline loyalty programs use region-based or dynamic pricing for award flights, charging the same number of miles whether you fly 200 miles or 2,000. British Airways uses distance-based pricing instead, which means shorter flights cost dramatically fewer Avios. Since BA is a Oneworld partner with American Airlines, you can use Avios to book AA-operated nonstop domestic flights. The result: a flight that AA might price at 12,500-25,000 miles can be booked for just 7,500 Avios through BA. This is one of the most reliable and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards.

Sign up for a free BA Executive Club account at ba.com. This is where your Avios balance lives and where you will search and book award flights on American Airlines.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, or Citi ThankYou Points to your BA Executive Club account. Transfers are typically instant. Only transfer what you need for a specific booking.

On the BA website, search for your route using the "Book with Avios" option. Look for American Airlines-operated nonstop flights. Filter results to find flights coded as AA with available Avios seats.

Confirm the flight is pricing at 7,500 Avios (under 1,151 miles) or 10,000 Avios (1,151-2,000 miles). Check that taxes and fees are the expected $5.60. If prices seem high, try different dates or check that you selected a nonstop flight.

Book the flight and add your AAdvantage number to the reservation so you receive any applicable elite benefits. You will receive a confirmation from British Airways, and the ticket will also appear in your AA account.

Yes. British Airways and American Airlines are both Oneworld alliance members, so you can use BA Avios to book award seats on AA-operated flights. You book directly through the British Airways website (ba.com) and search for AA flight numbers.

Flights under 1,151 miles cost 7,500 Avios each way in economy. Flights between 1,151-2,000 miles cost 10,000 Avios. Flights between 2,001-3,000 miles cost 12,500 Avios. The value proposition is strongest on the shortest flights where the Avios cost is lowest.

Not on domestic American Airlines flights. The typical fee is just $5.60 each way. High fuel surcharges only apply when booking British Airways-operated long-haul flights, not when using Avios on partner airlines like AA domestically.

Chase Ultimate Rewards, Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One Miles, and Citi ThankYou Points all transfer to British Airways Avios. Transfer ratios are 1:1 from Chase, Amex, and Capital One. Transfers are typically instant or within 24 hours.

This sweet spot was practically designed for the ChooseFI beginner — someone who has their first transferable points card (a Chase Sapphire Preferred, an Amex Gold, or a Bilt card) and wants to make a real, tangible redemption without navigating complex routing rules or praying for elusive premium cabin availability.

Minimum to get started: You need at least 7,500 Avios (or transferable points to convert) for a one-way. For a round-trip, 15,000. Most sign-up bonuses — even modest ones — cover multiple round-trips with this sweet spot.

Who this is NOT for: If you're flying coast-to-coast (NYC to LAX is over 2,400 miles — a different, higher Avios tier), this specific pricing won't apply. This sweet spot is purpose-built for short hops under 650 miles. It's also not the move if you already have AA elite status and can snag cheap upgrades — but for the rest of us, it's perfect.

This redemption earns a **5/5 for beginner friendliness** — and that rating is fully deserved. Let's be specific about why. The hardest part of most award bookings is finding available seats and navigating confusing partner systems. This one simplifies both: you're searching a major U.S. airline's (AA) domestic saver inventory, which is widely available on popular short-haul routes year-round. You're not hunting for a specific aircraft with lie-flat seats or hoping a single partner releases one business class seat. Domestic economy saver space is genuinely accessible. The booking process itself is two websites: aa.com to check availability, britishairways.com to book. Neither requires a phone call, neither has complicated routing rules for simple one-way or round-trip domestic bookings, and the transfer from Chase or Amex is instant. **The three things to get right:** 1. **Confirm saver availability on AA before transferring** — This habit protects you from the only real risk (irreversible point transfers). 2. **Verify the operating carrier is American Airlines, not British Airways** — One glance at 'Operated by' in the booking details handles this. 3. **Keep your BA Executive Club account active** — Set a reminder to log in or earn at least once every 36 months so your Avios don't expire. That's genuinely the whole checklist. If you've never booked an award flight before, this is the redemption to start with. You'll build the muscle memory — search, confirm, transfer, book — in about 20 minutes, and you'll have a nearly free flight to show for it. Welcome to travel rewards.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Using British Airways Avios for short domestic nonstop flights on American Airlines is one of the most practical and repeatable sweet spots in travel rewards. At just 7,500 Avios each way with $5.60 in fees, it dramatically undercuts what AA charges through its own program. With four major transfer partners feeding BA Avios, this sweet spot is accessible from virtually any points-earning strategy. Whether you are booking a quick NYC-Chicago hop or an LA-San Francisco shuttle, BA Avios should be your first look for short-haul domestic flights.

#8908. Black timber elements traverse concrete fragrance store in Tokyo

Mexican design firms Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts divided the interior of this concrete building in Tokyo, designed for perfume brand Xinú, with angular black-timber displays.

Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts designed the timber elements as sculptural interventions that also organise the interior of the three-storey shop, which is located in the city’s Aoyama neighbourhood.

The black-laminated wooden planks span the interior walls at jaunty angles, as if puncturing the building, which was originally designed by Japanese studio Satoshi Hirano.

“We approached the project as an intervention within an existing building, rather than simply designing an interior,” said Esrawe Studio founder Héctor Esrawe, who also co-founded Xinú.

“By introducing a continuous architectural structure that traverses its different levels, appearing and disappearing throughout the volume, we intended to generate a new perception of the original architecture,” he told Dezeen.

“Both structures coexist, establishing a dialogue between what was already there and what has been introduced, creating an unexpected spatial experience.”

Long, overlapping shelves with mirrored accents display products on the ground floor, which is dedicated to body perfume.

Xinú’s room scents are located on the first floor, where hand-painted brass panels on the walls and ceilings add a touch of warmth to the concrete and black-timber surfaces.

Aiming to reveal the processes behind the perfume products, the top floor displays botanical specimens, raw materials, found objects and collages in drawers.

Esrawe Studio also designed cabinet drawers to reference the storage and organisation typically found in natural history museums, intending to give visitors a feeling of discovery when interacting with the furniture.

“For Xinú, architecture has never been conceived simply as a backdrop for products, but as an essential part of how they are experienced,” said Esrawe.

“Our intention is to create spaces that encourage curiosity, discovery and a more intimate relationship with objects, materials and scent,” he continued.

“In Tokyo, the inserted architectural structures move beyond conventional retail display, becoming sculptural elements that enhance the presence of the objects.”

Xinú Tokyo is the latest branch Esrawe Studio and Cadena Concepts have designed for the perfume brand. Other shops include a radial wooden pavilion in Mexico City and a showroom in Oaxaca informed by basalt rock formations.
