#8846. How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

This story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

For three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

My mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

This was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the plans I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

They gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

My younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

The day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

On June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

The race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

By the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

My training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making plans; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

The trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.

#8845. Infographic | The Cost of Health “Optimization”

If you’re like most people, your answer is probably, “Yes!”

And, you probably want to live not only a longer life, but also a healthier one.

If so, you don’t have to look very far to find claims about how to improve—no, “optimize”—your health.

Want to reverse chronic disease? Extend that youthful glow? Live to 115… or forever? Lots of fitness influencers, authors, and podcasters will tell you how to do it.

But are their ultra-specific, advanced protocols necessary—or even effective?

And just how much effort, time, and money do these methods really require?

Most of all: Are the benefits worth the trade-offs?

By the end of it, you’ll have clarity about how to get the health and longevity you want, while living a life you enjoy.

#8844. How to Hold Yourself Accountable Without Beating Yourself Up

Here’s what that looks like inside real coaching conversations.

When most people picture “accountability,” they picture a drill sergeant.

Someone standing over you going “What were you thinking? Why did you skip that? Do you even want this?“

(And if there’s no drill sergeant handy, we do a pretty good job of beating ourselves up all on our own.)

Here’s the thing: if being hard on yourself worked, it would have worked by now.

Great accountability isn’t built on being a hard-ass.

It’s built on forward momentum and honest feedback.

The drill sergeant questions YOU. Your motivation. How much you want it.

Real accountability helps you try again quickly.

Then helps you see what you’re doing well and what can improve.

A client of mine had a hectic week. Travel, out of their routine, workouts missed.

The drill sergeant move is “why didn’t you do your workouts?!” at the exact moment they were already struggling.

“Hey! I know this has been a hectic week. Let’s do some push-ups together. Do a set next chance you get and shoot me a 👍. I’ll do one too.”

This got a 👍 and a “Thanks for the encouragement! This week has been so hectic my schedule got away from me.”

Then we build off of that by looking ahead to the next few days.

“How’s the rest of this week looking for strength training? I went ahead and put together a few variations in case you’re short on time.”

When you’re already struggling, the question isn’t “hey, why didn’t you do that?”

Then looking ahead to what’s coming up after that.

But forward momentum is only the first part of the equation.

The second step is giving honest feedback on both the wins AND the challenges.

To be a neutral observer. To point out what’s going well, what’s not, and suggest how we can improve it moving forward.

Based on the actual human in front of me: their unique goals, motivations, and whatever flavor of chaos they have going on in their own life (work, family, travel, illness, injury, etc.)

“Hey! I reviewed the strength workout on Friday. Solid work all around here. I can see from your form check video that you’re doing a better job staying balanced across your whole foot on the squat. 💪

I also noticed that the middle of the week has been tougher to get consistent workouts in. You’ve hit 2 out of the last 4 midweek workouts. I know work has been crazy with the project deadline you have coming up, so my guess is you’re getting buried and it makes it hard to get to the gym. Am I on the right track? I have some ideas for how we tackle that next week that I’ll drop down below in a video for you.”

This is the honest part. It didn’t go anywhere!

But instead of berating you for missing a workout, the goal is to look at all the evidence and suggest next steps.

Including if the evidence says that something BIG needs to change. It’s all on the table.

Accountability isn’t punishment for what you didn’t do.

It’s helping you decide what you do next.

If your week went haywire, before you beat yourself up, take this approach:

This is one piece of how our coaches do accountability. Here are a few more ideas for you:

Nerd Fitness cuts through the fitness B.S. to help people get stronger, healthier, and more confident – all with a fun, no-nonsense approach.

Humans featured are exceptional examples and do not guarantee individual success. Your experience and results may vary.

#8843. Zwift+ Adds a Virtual Coach and Real Roads to Your Indoor Rides

Zwift+ introduces a new subscription tier with an adaptive plan and real-road video. I tried both.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Since its 2015 debut, Zwift has focused on indoor riding in a gamified virtual world. Now the company is nudging riders toward the real world, too. Zwift+ introduces a new subscription tier with two big features: a virtual coach that sometimes tells you to ride outdoors, and video routes that let your avatar ride real roads while you stay indoors.

I’ve got all the details, along with my first impressions of riding the new routes and working with Coach.

Let me guess: You heard “new subscription tier,” sucked your teeth, and thought, “Oh, great. Another subscription. *Sigh* How much?” Friend, I feel you.

In the U.S., Zwift+ costs $29.99 a month, $10 more than the standard Zwift membership. It includes all the standard Zwift membership features, plus Coach and Video.

You can’t add just Coach or Video separately: they are a package deal. But the company says you can move between the standard membership and Zwift+ easily and as often as you like.

The standard Zwift membership remains $19.99 a month or $199.99 a year.

First of the two new big features in Zwift+ is Coach. It’s an adaptable virtual coaching service that builds easy-to-understand training plans.

Zwift isn’t going after the TrainingPeaks power user or even the AI-powered CoachCat audience. It is aimed at Zwifters who ride about three to eight hours a week and want more structure and a personalized plan without hiring a personal coach.

Coach lives in the Companion app. To build a plan, you answer a few straightforward questions: your experience level (recreational, amateur, competitive, or elite); your goal (train for an event, build endurance or speed, burn calories, or improve climbing); plan length (four, eight, or 12 weeks); how many hours you can ride each week; which days you’re available; and which day you can set aside for a longer ride.

Then it crunches a few 1s and 0s and spits out a plan.

While the shorthand version is that AI generates the plans, Zwift describes the planning engine as machine learning, a subset of artificial intelligence. Zwift says the plan comes from a training model grounded in peer-reviewed sports science and uses anonymized power and heart-rate data from millions of Zwift riders. It then adjusts the result to your goal, recent fitness, schedule, and riding preferences. The company says the model was tested against more than 65 million Zwift rides from 2025 and considers dozens of possible sessions when building a plan.

“The plan itself follows clear rules, so we can trace recommendations back to the reasons behind them. That was deliberate so that you can know why Coach tells you to ride something,” Mark Cote, Zwift’s head of product, told me.

The plans are Zwift-forward, naturally. They prescribe Zwift’s workouts, routes, RoboPacers, and events, with the occasional outdoor ride mixed in. Zwift says 63 percent of its riders do a variety of activities, while only 13 percent stick exclusively to structured workouts. Coach embraces variety and isn’t just weeks of ERG grind sessions.

Once your plan is set, you can see the schedule in the Companion app and the main app’s home screen. After the ride, you get feedback in a new Coach Analysis tab on the activity report. You can also check it later in Companion.

You can make changes in Companion, too: schedule a different Zwift ride or event, add an outdoor ride, or log a rest day or time away. Based on your changes, Coach can then adapt the plan at your request.

It can also notice when your week goes differently than planned. For example, if you take a rest day instead of doing a workout, record an outdoor ride through a linked service such as Garmin, or go too hard during an event, Coach may prompt you to adapt the plan. If you accept, it adjusts the plan.

Zwift says recovery data from services such as WHOOP and Oura can shape the wording of Coach’s messages, but a low recovery score won’t automatically change your prescribed workout. Coach Chat, an AI chatbot that would let you ask questions about the plan conversationally, is a future feature. It won’t be available at launch.

One noteworthy shortcoming of Zwift Coach: You can’t push Zwift workouts to a GPS head unit to perform them outdoors. That said, there are fairly easy ways to take the bones of a specific Zwift workout and make something that can live on your Hammerhead or Garmin head unit.

I’ve been using a beta version of Coach for a few weeks now. I’ve found it admirably easy to set up, use, and adapt. It’s all very Zwifty, with lots of colors, iconography, and cheery, easy-to-digest language.

The plans and workouts (Zwift has recently updated its library with dozens of new workouts) seem well considered, but I don’t have enough time with Coach to know how effective it is at lifting my performance.

For someone taking their first steps toward structured training and feedback, I think Zwift Coach is a brilliant entry point, and I feel even more experienced cyclists looking to improve their performance will appreciate how easy and user-friendly Coach is.

The second highlight new feature is Zwift Video. It adds real roads to the game: Your avatar rides over footage recorded on actual routes, with familiar Zwift physics and game features layered on top.

At launch, 21 routes across six countries total 385 kilometers (239 miles) of roads. The routes range from 6.2 to 29 kilometers (about 3.9 to 18 miles) and include the French Alps, Mallorca, Tenerife, the Western Cape, Lofoten, southern Utah, Colorado, and the Scottish Highlands. Zwift says it will begin adding more routes regularly in the new year.

Zwift employees have recorded the footage specifically for Zwift’s video routes. Playback speeds up or slows down with your avatar, and like classic Zwift, you’ll still see other Zwifter avatars and find all the familiar Zwift features, including drafting, segment leaderboards, HoloReplay, PowerUps, Ride Ons, Drops, XP, and badges. Pack dynamics and road surfaces retain the same ride characteristics as in Zwift’s classic graphics-based worlds. Surfaces range from smooth pavement to broken pavement and gravel, with different rolling resistance.

The main restriction is that video routes are one-way. You can’t make a U-turn, and the roads don’t loop. Reach the end, and you are teleported back to the start where your ride continues uninterrupted.

I’ve ridden a few of the video routes so far. The rideplay is familiar Zwift, so it’s really just a change of scenery. And beautiful scenery it is. I’ve ridden a few of these routes in the real world, and while they can’t compare with the real thing, they are still often breathtaking in Zwift. There’s plenty to see, including quirky little details that I’m certain will become part of Zwift lore.

One welcome change is how Zwift marks the start of segments. Large chevrons “painted” on the road alert you to an approaching segment, and barriers and more chevrons clearly mark the start line. It’s a huge improvement over the sometimes easy-to-miss segment starts in Zwift’s classic worlds. I asked a Zwift representative whether classic-world segments might get similar treatment, and they said it was under consideration.

A couple of details take some getting used to. Cars and trucks appear in the footage. Zwift says it curates the footage to reduce traffic, but the roads aren’t traffic-free; however, the traffic doesn’t influence the game’s physics.

Climbing also looks different. I found that a 10 percent grade on a video route looked much less steep than the same grade in a classic Zwift world. A Zwift representative told me classic routes visually exaggerate grades, roughly doubling them, so the climbs read clearly on screen. Video footage doesn’t get that treatment, and the camera can flatten the terrain.

At launch, Video won’t have meetups or scheduled events, but Zwift says those will arrive in the coming months.

Now you might be thinking, wait, didn’t Zwift buy Rouvy, an indoor riding and training service built around real-world video routes? It did. But even though Zwift owns Rouvy, these aren’t Rouvy routes. Zwift representatives told me the video routes were filmed exclusively for Zwift and that the two services will continue independently, with their own content and features. They said there are no plans to bring Rouvy content to Zwift or fold Rouvy into the platform.

Zwift+ isn’t the only change coming. Zwift is also refreshing the Companion home screen, adding WHOOP and Oura connections, and introducing Watt Lock, an ERG-style control that lets you lock onto a target power during free rides.

Zwift also opened The Wild Isles, a new Watopia expansion, on October 26. Inspired by California’s coast and Catalina Island, it adds three islands and about 17 kilometers of flat roads between the Mayan Jungle and Jarvis Island. The new roads create a bypass around the Jungle and include nine cycling routes and three running routes, with ocean views and wildlife such as bison, whales, and egrets.

A gear editor for his entire career, Matt’s journey to becoming a leading cycling tech journalist started in 1995, and he’s been at it ever since; likely riding more cycling equipment than anyone on the planet along the way. Previous to his time with Bicycling, Matt worked in bike shops as a service manager, mechanic, and sales person. Based in Durango, Colorado, he enjoys riding and testing any and all kinds of bikes, so you’re just as likely to see him on a road bike dressed in Lycra at a Tuesday night worlds ride as you are to find him dressed in a full face helmet and pads riding a bike park on an enduro bike. He doesn’t race often, but he’s game for anything; having entered road races, criteriums, trials competitions, dual slalom, downhill races, enduros, stage races, short track, time trials, and gran fondos. Next up on his to-do list: a multi day bikepacking trip, and an e-bike race.

#8842. Over a Tenth of Your Clients Are Dealing With IBS—And Here’s How to Help

This is according to the results of a study of nearly 2,000 people with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).1

In other research, people with IBS said they would take a medicine that carried a one percent risk of sudden death if it would cure their symptoms2—which can include urgent bouts of diarrhea, gas, or persistent constipation.

Some people with IBS experience bouts of abdominal pain they describe as worse than childbirth. These flare-ups can siphon concentration, interrupt sleep, and destroy work productivity.3

As a result, many people with IBS plan their lives around the availability of private, clean bathrooms. Fear of a sudden flare-up leads some to avoid restaurants, get-togethers, even exercising in public.

This pervading worry has a name—gastrointestinal-specific anxiety—and it can affect everything from social relationships to overall well-being. It’s also the main reason people with IBS report worse quality of life than people with other chronic conditions, including heart disease, diabetes, and end-stage kidney disease.4

PN Super Coach Sarah Maughan, certified through Monash University—a global leader in understanding the link between food sensitivities and IBS—has witnessed how lifestyle changes can prevent flare-ups, calm GI anxiety, and allow people with IBS to live the lives they want.

“My hope is for everyone with IBS to know they have options, whether that’s turning to a physician for medication and/or a health coach to learn about lifestyle changes and how to put them into action,” says Maughan.

In this article, we’ll hear more from Maughan. You’ll also learn:

Plus, if you’re a health coach, you’ll learn how to support clients with IBS while safely staying within your scope of practice.

Sometimes referred to as “spastic colon,” IBS is the most commonly diagnosed digestive disorder in the world, affecting about 14 percent percent of adults.5

Unlike Crohn’s and other inflammatory bowel diseases (IBD), IBS doesn’t alter the architecture of the gut. When healthcare professionals use diagnostic imaging, they find no infections, inflammation, damage to the bowel wall, or other evidence of disease.

Years ago, this lack of visible disease led many healthcare professionals to assume that IBS was purely psychological. More recently, however, this thinking has shifted.

Experts now view IBS as a functional neuro-gastrointestinal disorder.

That means the nerves between the GI tract and the brain don’t function optimally, causing the brain to deliver unnecessary pain signals and interfere with typical bowel function.

IBS symptoms can come and go, with some people experiencing months or years of relief only to suffer a severe flare-up that can last hours to weeks.

In addition, not everyone with IBS experiences the same set of symptoms, which can make the condition challenging to diagnose.

The below illustration shows the range of IBS symptoms.

Researchers are still trying to understand why the gut functions differently in people with IBS. However, they do have a few theories.

According to one hypothesis, the nerve endings in the GI tract may be overly sensitive in people with IBS. This can lead to two different sets of symptoms.

▶ Hypersensitive nerves communicate pain signals to the brain, causing people with IBS to notice digestive processes that other people wouldn’t feel. Tiny gas bubbles may be severely uncomfortable for someone with IBS, for example, but not bother someone without the disorder.

▶ Overreactive nerves can trigger GI muscles to contract with too much force, leading to gas, bloating, and diarrhea. If they underreact, the same muscles don’t contract forcefully enough, which slows the passage of food through the intestine and leads to constipation.

Another theory blames disturbances on the gut microbiome, which helps to explain why some people develop IBS symptoms after first having a severe GI illness like the Norovirus.

If you or your client suspect IBS, see a credentialed health professional.

The symptoms of IBS overlap with several other gastrointestinal diseases and health conditions that can require medication, surgery, or medically-supervised lifestyle changes. These include infections, inflammatory bowel diseases, celiac disease, cancer, and food allergies, among others.

It’s especially important to see a medical professional if you or your client notice any of the following:

In addition to ruling out other GI conditions, a healthcare professional will also ask detailed questions about you or your client’s symptoms. This information allows them to pinpoint which IBS “type” you or your client might have:

You or your client’s IBS type will inform what your healthcare professional recommends.

A healthcare provider might suggest a short course of antibiotics and antidiarrheal medicine for IBS-D. On the other hand, for IBS-C, they might recommend a fiber supplement, non-habit-forming laxative, laxative-like medication, or other medicine that reduces the perception of pain and regulates bowel movements.

In order to get the most out of the visit, you can help your client (or yourself) prepare for a healthcare appointment.

A healthcare professional will likely ask the following questions, so consider the responses beforehand:

Another way to prepare for your first appointment?

Well, you might not like it, but it’s a good idea to…

Consider keeping a poo diary for a couple of weeks before your appointment.

In the diary, track the frequency of bowel movements and other symptoms. Use the Bristol Stool Chart (below) to take note of the quality of your poo. This information can help your healthcare professional assess whether you have IBS and which type.

(To learn more about the clues your poos can hide, read: 6 reasons you should care about your poop health)

In recent years, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration approved several new prescription medicines for IBS, along with a medical device that stimulates the cranial nerves behind the ear.

In addition, thousands of research papers have looked at the interaction between IBS and various lifestyle habits, with many promising findings.

Here are five evidence-based ways to reduce the symptoms of IBS (and bonus, many of them are great for enhancing overall health too).

People with IBS who exercise regularly tend to experience fewer symptoms and flare-ups than people who don’t exercise.

When researchers asked people with IBS to walk moderately for an hour three times a week, study participants experienced significant relief from bloating and abdominal pain within 12 weeks.6

How exercise soothes IBS isn’t fully understood, though.

According to other research, exercise may reduce stress and improve mental health, which, in turn, may help improve communication between the gut and the brain.7 8

Another theory argues that exercise helps encourage the growth of health-promoting gut bacteria, which may help to break down food more efficiently and decrease inflammation.9

Anxiety, stress, and depression all activate stress hormones like norepinephrine (noradrenaline) and cortisol, which can:

Of course, stress doesn’t come with an on/off switch.

Simply telling yourself, “Stop getting so stressed out!” won’t likely help—and may even paradoxically lead to more stress.

That’s why Precision Nutrition-certified coaches like Maughan help clients learn to focus on what’s within their control—such as practicing self-compassion, or experimenting with nervous system regulators like yoga, breathing exercises, and gentle walking.

As the image below illustrates, clients can control how they perceive, respond to, and anticipate stressors—but not always the stressors themselves.

Either way, when clients focus more on what they can control and less on what they can’t, they often feel calmer and more capable.

(If you want to help a client figure out just what’s within their control—and what’s not—try out our free worksheet: Sphere of Control Worksheet)

(Assess your current stress load by taking our free quiz: Do you have a Stress Bod?)

PN coaches have long appreciated and advocated slower, more relaxed eating.

Yes, slow eating helps people fill up on fewer calories—but it also tends to help clients reduce or even eliminate GI woes like acid reflux, bloating, and pain.

For one, slower eating often translates to more chewing. In addition to mechanically mashing food into a pulp, increased chewing also allows the mouth’s digestive enzymes to pre-digest food. As a result, the stomach and intestines have to work less hard.

Plus, eating in a relaxed setting often lowers stress hormones like norepinephrine and cortisol, making it less likely that they will intensify GI pain signals.

According to Maughan, this can be especially important for young parents, as it’s not always easy to eat undistracted and peacefully when tending to little ones.

(Sounds simple, but slow eating is more challenging than people think—and a lot more impactful. Learn more: Try the slow-eating 30-day challenge.)

According to research, people with IBS experience more shallow, less restorative, and more interrupted sleep.13

Because of poor sleep quality, many people with IBS sleep more hours overall than people without IBS—yet feel less rested.

Fatigue can then set off a vicious cycle. When people don’t sleep restfully, stress hormone levels tend to be higher, which can exacerbate gut pain.14

Unrested people also tend to feel hungrier during the day. Cravings for fats and sweets also intensify, driving people to reach for the very foods more likely to trigger IBS symptoms—and wolf them down too quickly.

As with stress, you can’t simply will yourself to sleep more restfully.

However, the first three strategies—exercise, stress management, and slower eating—can all help.

Some PN clients have found that consuming a smaller dinner earlier in the evening gives their bodies more time to digest before bed. Other clients tell us that a relaxing pre-bedtime routine—a few minutes of foam rolling, a guided meditation, a bath, or some journalling—tends to help.

(Find out the best practices for getting better sleep by checking out our infographic: The power of sleep)

While there’s no one-size-fits-all IBS diet, experts have identified several food categories that are more likely to be problematic for many people. These include:

▶ Fermentable Oligosaccharides, Disaccharides, Monosaccharides, and Polyols (FODMAPs), which are a family of carbohydrate-rich foods that are poorly absorbed in the small intestine. Even in people without IBS, these foods tend to slow digestion and attract water. When gut bacteria ferment them, they produce gas, which can stretch the intestinal wall. For most, this slowed digestion and gas isn’t especially noticeable; In people with IBS, it can lead to intense pain. High-FODMAP foods include wheat, rye, barley, onions, garlic, beans, dairy, honey, cashews, some processed meats, and many fruits and vegetables. (More about FODMAPs in the next section.)

▶ Caffeinated beverages and foods, especially coffee, which trigger the release of stress hormones, stimulate the production of stomach acid, increase muscle contractions in the colon, and irritate the lining of the intestine.15

▶ Alcohol and spicy foods that irritate the gut.16 17

▶ High fructose corn syrup and sugar alcohols such sorbitol and mannitol, which have been linked to gas, bloating, and diarrhea in susceptible people.18 19

▶ Fatty, greasy foods, which can slow digestion and attract water, leading to loose stools, bloating, and gas.20 21

If the idea of giving up all the foods and beverages on the above list has you in a cold sweat, know this…

Not everyone with IBS is sensitive to the same foods and beverages.

“Everyone can have different triggers,” says Maughan. “That’s why it’s so important to figure out what makes your body feel good and what doesn’t.”

Some people struggle with apples but are okay with berries. Others can drink green tea but not black. One person might be able to consume five to eight ounces of beer but not 12. A gluten-free diet may work great for some but not others.

Similarly, many people find relief by avoiding certain high-FODMAP foods. However, you may only be sensitive to some FODMAPs and not others. If so, eliminating all FODMAPs would be unnecessarily restrictive and difficult to follow consistently.

For this reason, it can be helpful to try an elimination diet to see which foods and beverages are problematic—along with the quantities you can safely tolerate, says Maughan. You’ll learn more about elimination diets in the next section.

(Want someone to walk you through exactly how to do an elimination diet? Read: How and why to do an elimination diet.)

In our online coaching communities, we often see people asking some version of the following question:

“My client just told me that she has IBS. Am I allowed to continue to coach this person?”

As we mentioned, Maughan specializes in helping people with digestive problems. Coaching someone with IBS is no different than coaching a client with any other nutritional goal, she says.

“Because IBS is often largely associated with what someone eats, it’s within a coach’s wheelhouse—with some caveats,” says Maughan. “You can’t diagnose your client with the condition, and you should make it clear that you’re not prescribing a diet for them. In addition, you should encourage clients to seek care from a medical professional, especially if you suspect something other than IBS is going on.”

To stay within your scope of practice, follow these do’s and don’ts.

Elimination diets do what the name suggests: They exclude certain foods for a short period—usually three weeks. Then, you slowly reintroduce specific foods and monitor your symptoms for possible reactions.

Elimination diets work a lot like a science experiment that helps you identify problematic foods.

The phrase “elimination diet” may sound scary and off-putting, as if you’ll be living for months on bland food you have to slurp through a straw.

However, there are many different types of elimination diets, with some much less restrictive than others.

This is an excellent option for people who suspect they already know which foods and beverages trigger symptoms.

It goes like this: You eliminate up to four foods for several weeks. Then, slowly reintroduce them one at a time to see if your symptoms return.

Let’s say, for example, from experience, you know you feel bad whenever you eat dairy. On the lite elimination diet, you’d eliminate just dairy for three weeks. Then you’d reintroduce it to see how you feel.

If you’re unsure of how food interacts with your GI tract—but aren’t ready for a super restrictive eating plan, our Precision Nutrition elimination diet is likely the way to go.

Created by PN and approved by several registered dietitians, the plan removes many of the foods most likely to cause problems, while still including a variety of vegetables, fruits, starches, legumes, nuts, seeds, and meats, so you can continue to eat a well-balanced diet.

To learn more, download our FREE Ultimate Guide to Elimination Diets. This ebook has everything you need to be successful, including an at-a-glance chart that helps you easily follow the diet, along with recipes, meal ideas, and tip sheets.

Over several years, researchers at Monash University in Australia have developed and extensively studied a low-FODMAP elimination diet for people with IBS.22

Unlike other types of elimination diets, the FODMAP diet is a highly specialized form of medical nutrition therapy. The FODMAP diet’s list of problematic foods (shown below) is anything but intuitive, and the reintroduction phase is more complex than other elimination diets.

As a result, if you’ve been diagnosed with IBS and suspect you have a FODMAP issue, seek the expertise of a FODMAP-certified practitioner. You can also download Monash University’s FODMAP Diet app, which will help you navigate low-FODMAP eating.

In isolation, more knowledge doesn’t always lead to more power.

For example, there’s a difference between knowing that dairy messes with your gut and doing something with that knowledge.

Similarly, you might know that you feel better when you eat a small dinner earlier in the evening, but you may struggle to plan your life so an early dinner happens regularly.

This is where a certified health coach can help.

“Many of my clients already have an idea of the foods that tend to cause them problems,” says Maughan, “But they’re nervous to know for sure because they fear that the knowledge will make eating more challenging.”

Even if you do an elimination diet and you learn your favorite food is contributing to your IBS, you don’t have to do anything with that information.

You can choose to continue to eat your favourite foods if you want, AND you can choose to avoid them when it’s really important for you not to experience IBS symptoms, she says.

“With knowledge, you have choices,” says Maughan.

#8841. I Used to Buy Cycling Kit for How It Looked. Now I Buy It for How It Gets Me Through the Ride—My Three Rules for Cycling Kit

Versatility, comfort, and durability matter most when choosing kit that improves your ride.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

After spending almost two decades riding and years running bike shops, I have narrowed down my priorities for key criteria when buying cycling apparel. I’m looking for a product that is durable, performs well in varying conditions, and is comfortable over miles on the bike.

Apparel falls into different categories depending on the rider. For some, it falls into a category of fashion. Those riders want their choice of apparel to tell a story about who they are on the bike.

For other riders, safety is the biggest driving factor. This group is intentionally easy to see by their bright colors riding by. While other riders solely look for a great deal, digging through clearance racks at bike shops as the seasons change.

Finding kit that performs the way we want our bike to perform can give us a better experience on our ride compared to getting whatever the cool kids are wearing—just for fashion’s sake. Here I’m going to dive deeper into each of the priorities I have for my jerseys and bibs to shed some light on why there’s value in this shift—especially this time of year.

What I look for in a jersey, especially for fall, is one that will vent well on the way up, but keep me comfortable on the way back down. I love a good gilet, especially leaving it open on the way down a road. If my jersey can do what the gilet does then that’s one less piece of kit I have to buy and bring. Lately I’ve been using the Dottore Hybrid Long Sleeve jersey from Q36.5 and it checks off all those boxes.

I tried this jersey out on a recent trip to Italy where we had a roughly 2,500-foot climb followed immediately by an equal descent. The temperature was hovering around the mid-fifties and usually, I would bring a vest for a ride like this. However, I was told this jersey should be perfect for these conditions, so I wanted to give it a proper test. On the way up I didn’t feel a need to unzip the jersey at all and on the screaming descent I never felt cold. Somehow Q36.5 figured out how to give the best of both worlds in one jersey.

Many of us think of a good pair of bibs being the key component to comfort on the bike—and in some ways that’s not wrong. Comfort on your sit bones can be greatly improved by getting the right saddle and sometimes a bike fit to determine what that saddle is and how the saddle should be positioned. But a good pair of bibs can still greatly improve comfort on the bike even after you get a fit and get the right saddle.

Not all chamois pads are created equal, and not all bibs hold the chamois in the place you need after miles of pedaling. Part of the challenge with bibs is you don’t really know until you get on the bike to ride—and good bibs aren’t exactly an inexpensive purchase.

“An unlined full length bib like the Velocio Luxe Tights offers a more comfortable go to bib for when you need to cover you legs but don't need to have fleece warmth,” says Trevor Raab, our resident bike racer and photographer at Bicycling. What I typically look for in bibs is a pair with minimal seams, has a chamois pad that offers both padding and ventilation, and good support and structure from the overalls to help hold the bib in place.

The final piece of my puzzle for gear and apparel is durability. Part of the reality is that just like bikes, apparel has pieces that are more consumable than others and will need to be replaced over time.

I’m someone who tends to stress test both bikes and apparel from hitting the ground. I haven’t found any apparel that holds up to a good impact to the pavement or gravel— as can be seen by many of my bibs having a tear on one of the hips. However, not all material holds up the same over time.

From the bibs that I have tried I either haven’t put enough miles in them or I have put over a year of miles on them and there is a noticeable impact to the comfort of the chamois. But something to note: more padding isn’t inherently better in a chamois. From a durability perspective and my experience, the thicker pads compress over time and aren’t necessarily more comfortable on the bike. The pair I’ve gotten the most miles on this year are the Q36.5 Dottore Bib Shorts. I’ve put a few hundred miles in them and they are still as comfortable as the first ride. Every rider I talk to that has tried this pair of bibs has experienced the same thing.

It’s important to acknowledge the pricing of some of this high-end kit is not a small investment. Shifting your perspective of apparel as just clothes to looking at apparel as gear can make it easier to understand. Too many times when I worked in a shop someone would spend thousands of dollars on a bike only to buy low-priced apparel. There’s nothing wrong with buying entry-level kit to get started. But if you are someone who spends thousands on your bike, then it’s likely ride quality matters to you regardless of the price. If you start to think about your apparel as gear, it’s easier to see that great apparel can impact your ride just like riding on a great bike.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
